readings.evolution:
What's tested
  • The seven basic types of dental implants, and how to recognize each one on a radiograph or photo
  • Why early materials (gold, lead, porcelain, stainless steel) failed, and why titanium works
  • How osseointegration was discovered, and the old five-year success standard
  • The problems of subperiosteal, blade, ramus frame and transosteal implants

Dr. Leonard Mueninghoff is a retired professor and prosthodontist who ran UAB's graduate prosthodontics program and has been at the school about 38 years. He treated patients with every kind of implant in this lecture, many of them placed decades ago. He said up front what matters for the exam: the seven types of implants, and being able to recognize them. "Out of this entire lecture, that's something that you really need to know." The stories around them are for context: he doesn't want you memorizing "a lot of worthless things," only to be familiar enough to say "I've heard of that" when one walks into your chair.

Early materials: why they failed

People tried to replace roots long before titanium. In 1809 someone used gold roots; in 1888, lead; in the 1800s, platinum; in 1891, porcelain; around 1900, iridium and gold again. Gold and platinum failed for the same reason: they form very little surface oxide. Today's titanium implants are covered by a layer of titanium oxide, which is a ceramic, and the bone actually integrates with that oxide, not with the metal itself. Porcelain may have integrated, but the porcelain of the time wasn't strong enough and broke under load.

Titanium and the discovery of osseointegration

Osseointegration was discovered by a physician, not a dentist. Per-Ingvar Brånemark, a Swedish orthopedic surgeon, put small titanium chambers into animals to study bone and blood flow; when he tried to remove them, they wouldn't come off, because the bone had grown onto the titanium. Brånemark's name and the root form implant became synonymous. In the United States, Carl Misch popularized implants and wrote the textbook this course leans on. Dr. Mueninghoff added a caution from a radiologist relative: titanium is not completely inert immunologically, though no clinical problem has shown up in decades of use.

The seven basic types

When Dr. Mueninghoff arrived at UAB he saw all seven in patients. They are getting rarer as those patients age, but you may still meet them. Most are named for where they sit relative to the bone:

  • Subperiosteal: a metal framework that lies on the bone, under the periosteum.
  • Endodontic stabilizer: a rod run through the root canal of a tooth and out the apex into the bone.
  • Transosseous (transosteal): goes through the bone, in practice the anterior mandible.
  • Intramucosal insert: little buttons on a denture that snap into holes in the mucosa.
  • Blade and plate form: a flat metal blade set into a slot in the bone.
  • Mandibular ramus frame: one piece running from the symphysis back into both rami.
  • Root form: the screw-shaped titanium implant used today.

Endodontic stabilizers and pins

An endodontic stabilizer is a rod run all the way through the root canal and out the root end into the bone, to steady a weak tooth. The ones Dr. Mueninghoff saw were mobile and had to be removed with grafting. They failed for two reasons: they were surgical stainless steel, not titanium (one looked like nickel-chrome-beryllium), and the seal where the rod left the tooth was poor, so the root canal failed. Some dentists drove several pins into the bone at different angles and joined them with acrylic as an abutment; those patients came in with chronic infections. When titanium implants first arrived, patients who had heard about these devices didn't want "an implant" at all.

Intramucosal inserts

Intramucosal inserts were small buttons on the tissue side of a denture, usually a palateless upper denture, so it caused less gagging. The dentist marked soft spots in the palatal mucosa, drilled small holes into the mucosa with a large round acrylic bur, and told the patient not to take the denture out for two weeks. The tissue healed around the buttons and held the denture. The catch: the patient could not leave the denture out more than a few hours, or the holes began to close.

The mandibular ramus frame

The ramus frame is a one-piece implant designed to retain a mandibular complete denture. It runs from the symphysis back into both rami, with a bar over the ridge. It was designed by Drs. Harold and Ralph Roberts (about 1970), California brothers who were tinkerers and made the first ones in their garage. In Birmingham, Dr. H. Ford Turner, an anatomist who became a dentist, placed them so carefully (he didn't burn the bone and he cleaned the metal) that his patients kept them 10 to 25 years, when most lasted only a few. A plunger called a Lew attachment snapped through or under the bar to hold the denture. Patients needed them because a flat mandible under a loose lower denture kept resorbing, sometimes until it fractured. Problems: infection in the ramus area, and when big implants fail, they fail big.

Subperiosteal implants

Exactly what the name says: the framework sits under the periosteum, on top of the bone. The surgeon laid back the tissue and periosteum, took an impression of the bone, sutured, had a lattice made, then reopened days later to set it and sutured again: two surgeries, which Dr. Mueninghoff called brutal. They were loaded right away and often hooked to natural teeth. Some lasted close to 10 years, but when they failed they caused gross bone destruction ("when they went south, they really went south"). Later designs added a hydroxyapatite coating, and a custom titanium subperiosteal from Cleveland left healthy tissue, another sign that the body likes titanium.

Blade implants

The Roberts brothers also originated the blade (late 1960s): a solid flat blade set in a slot cut in the bone. Linkow put holes in it (the Blade-Vent), and Cranin cut the bottom like an anchor (the Anchor blade). The early ones were not titanium, usually had a soft tissue layer between metal and bone instead of osseointegration, and were usually hooked to a natural tooth, which is what really held them. Success depended heavily on the surgeon's skill: a sharp bur, water cooling and going slowly. Some were successful.

Success before Brånemark

"Figures don't lie, but liars figure." Before Brånemark, an implant counted as a success if it was in functional service for five years in 75% of patients. One patient arrived with blades from the "Turner Clinic" in Cleveland (not Ford Turner) that were held in only by years of antibiotics, kept going to pass the five-year mark.

Transosteal implants

A transosteal (transosseous) implant goes through the bone. The idea started in Germany in the 1930s. The best known is the transmandibular implant (TMI) of Bosker: a plate under the chin with posts through the anterior mandible into the mouth, made of a soft, high-gold alloy, joined by a bar. UAB placed many before root forms were approved, mostly for patients whose mandible was so thin (about 5 mm or less) it was at risk of fracture; Medicare paid for a bone plate, and Dr. Peter Waite realized the plate could extend into the mouth. It was done in the operating room through the chin, and the bar was delivered within 24 hours. The bar was retained with Hader clips (nylon: white, then yellow, then red as the bar wears) or a metal-to-metal Dolder bar (no longer used). A striking result: the bone behind the plate grew thicker, a lesson that force keeps bone healthy.

Other materials and designs

  • Stainless steel, nickel-chrome and vitreous carbon were all tried; vitreous carbon broke up.
  • Hollow basket implants hoped bone would grow through their holes; bone only grows about half a millimeter in.
  • Core-Vent cemented its abutments into the implant, so a broken one couldn't be unscrewed and had to be ground out. Normally an abutment screw torqued to about 35 Ncm can be backed out, even with a periodontal probe if it has loosened.
  • Single crystal sapphire (Japan) integrated well, since it is all ceramic oxide, but wasn't strong enough and broke.
  • The IMZ (intramobile cylinder) had a plastic insert meant to act like a periodontal ligament when the implant was joined to a tooth; it moved so much that it damaged the tooth, and it had only micro-retention from its surface, no macro-retention.
  • Frialit (Dentsply) was wider at the top and narrower at the bottom, to load the crestal bone and avoid stress shielding (long 16 mm implants lost crestal bone down to about 12 mm).

What we learned

Osseointegration turned out far stronger than anyone expected. Early on, a 12 mm implant seemed short and 14 mm was better; today 10, 8 and even 6 mm implants are used. There are about 173 implant companies worldwide, so pick two or three systems and stick with them. To identify an unknown implant from a radiograph, use a site such as whatimplantisthat.com, which asks questions and narrows it down. And "think periodontics": an implant needs enough bone, in quantity and quality, and attached tissue around it, just like a tooth.
readings.intro:
What's tested
  • What a dental implant is, and what osseointegration means
  • Primary and secondary osseointegration (stability), and healing times in the mandible and maxilla
  • One-stage vs two-stage surgery (Schroeder vs Brånemark), with the cover screw and healing abutment
  • Endosteal, eposteal (subperiosteal) and transosteal implants, and which family the blade and ramus frame belong to
  • How to tell a healthy implant from a failing one, and the causes of failure
  • Titanium: the oxide layer, commercially pure grades vs Ti-6Al-4V, and each school system's material and surface
  • Machined (screw) vs smooth (cylinder) implants, and additive vs subtractive surface treatments
  • Periodontal attachment vs peri-implant attachment, biologic width, and why an implant is not a tooth

Dr. Ramakiran Chavali (Restorative Sciences) opens the course. Its goals: learn the basics of restoring a single implant and of implant surgery, the history and science of implants, imaging, the ADA codes, treatment planning for simple cases, and the three systems the school's clinic uses: Nobel Biocare (Conical Connection), Straumann (Bone Level) and BioHorizons (Tapered Internal). BioHorizons is an Alabama company that started at UAB. In the PCD lab you restore an implant at #9: alginate impression, wax-up, radiographic and surgical guides, an impression of the implant and a provisional. His recording is from an earlier year; the second half of the lecture, the implant-tissue interface, comes from his slides.

What is a dental implant?

The slide's definition: "A prosthetic device made of alloplastic material(s) implanted into the oral tissues beneath the mucosal or/and periosteal layer, and on/or within the bone to provide retention and support for a fixed or removable dental prosthesis." For a single tooth, the bone is prepared, the implant placed and allowed to heal; then an abutment goes on the implant and a crown on the abutment.

What implants are used for

  • Single crowns and fixed bridges: for example implants at #3, #4 and #5, placed in two stages, then healing abutments, custom abutments and crowns.
  • Removable partial dentures: an RPD gets its retention, stability and support from teeth and ridge and can flop around where back teeth are missing; implants with attachments under it give significantly higher retention, stability, support and esthetics.
  • Complete dentures: "A two-implant-retained overdenture is considered standard of care in rehabilitation of an edentulous mandible." UAB calls it 2-2-2: two dentures, two implants, two attachments. The gold-colored Locator abutments click into nylon inserts in metal housings in the denture; they retain it but aren't a rigid fixation. A well-made maxillary denture holds by suction; the mandibular one is unstable because of the tongue and muscle attachments, which is why the implants go in the mandible.
  • Fixed dentures: several implants joined by a bar, with the denture fixed to it; only the dentist can remove it.

Osseointegration

In 1952, Brånemark, an orthopedic surgeon, found that titanium chambers he had put in rabbit bone were difficult to remove; in the 1960s he coined the term osseointegration for the stable, functional bond between titanium screws and living bone. The slide's definition: "the apparent direct attachment or connection of osseous tissue to an inert, alloplastic material without intervening connective tissue."

The surgeon drills a channel (an osteotomy) with sequential drill bits. The implant is slightly wider than the last drill, and bone is a little elastic, so the implant locks in mechanically, like a screw in a wall: that is primary stability. Then the body remodels: cells remove some of the bone that was there at surgery and lay down new bone in the pattern of the implant. That is secondary stability, and it is osseointegration proper.

  • Primary osseointegration: the initial bone healing between the implant and the osteotomy.
  • Secondary osseointegration: the bone remodeling phase, the critical factor for long-term success (from about 4-6 weeks after initial healing, and it continues after the implant is loaded).
  • Osseointegration is dynamic and progressive, and success can't be judged until the implant is loaded.

A video in the lecture walked through the biology (blood clot, platelets, neutrophils, macrophages, angiogenesis). He won't ask about the cells; the point to take from it is that from about day 7, osteoclasts resorb the bone edges and primary stability drops, while woven bone forms on the implant and secondary stability rises. Under the electron microscope a thin protein layer lies between bone and titanium. Woven bone later remodels into lamellar bone, oriented perpendicular to the thread peaks.

How long to wait

The mandible is generally dense and the maxilla less so (like solid oak vs styrofoam, though everyone differs). The traditional wait, and what you'll do in the second-floor clinic unless the surgeon says otherwise: about 4 months in the mandible and 6 months in the maxilla. Surgeons often quote other times (3 months, for example), depending on the system and protocol.

Wolff's law and loading

Wolff's law: the internal architecture of bone is determined by the external forces on it. Within an adaptive window of load, bone gets stronger (people who lift weights have stronger bones). Too little load and it atrophies: after an extraction the alveolar bone, the bone that holds the tooth, keeps resorbing toward the basal bone. Too much load, as in parafunction or bruxism, also loses bone. Implants are very sensitive to force, so once a crown or denture goes on, the occlusion is adjusted so the implant isn't overworked.

Implants can sometimes be loaded or provisionalized right away, mainly for esthetics in a few cases. He described the conditions: high insertion torque (he said at least about 50 Ncm in that recording; the terminology lecture gives the consensus number), a patient without systemic problems such as diabetes, and a low-force site such as an incisor, with splinting to spread the force. Even then the occlusion on the provisional is kept light. He said he won't ask which cases qualify for immediate loading.

One-stage vs two-stage surgery

"I'll ask you a question about single-stage surgery and two-stage surgery."

  • Two-stage (Brånemark, 1985): the implant is placed, a cover screw goes on and the flap is closed, so the implant is submerged, isolated from the mouth, for 3-6 months. A second surgery uncovers it and places a healing abutment, and the soft tissue is closed around it.
  • One-stage (Schroeder, 1996): a non-submerged technique with transmucosal healing; a healing abutment goes on at placement, so the implant sticks out into the mouth from day one, with a shorter healing period of 3-4 months and no second surgery.
  • Either way, the soft tissue needs at least 3 weeks to heal around the healing abutment before the final impression.
  • Choose two-stage when healing is a concern (a diabetic patient, for example: close it and let the implant heal in a sterile environment); one-stage suits a young, healthy patient with good hygiene, good primary stability and good keratinized mucosa.

Types of implants

The classification is by where the implant sits relative to the bone:

  • Endosteal (endosseous): in the bone. The most commonly used; placed into the alveolar and/or basal bone of the mandible or maxilla, and it transects only one cortical plate. It doesn't come out the other side. Endosteal implants include the root form (most common; mimics the shape of roots for load distribution), the blade form and the ramus frame. Blade and ramus frame implants had excessive bone loss and increased failure rates and aren't used anymore. His "tricky question": a blade is endosseous, not transosteal or subperiosteal.
  • Eposteal (subperiosteal): on the bone. The frame sits directly beneath the periosteum over the bony cortex. Problems: difficult retrievability, extensive surgery, excessive bone loss; when they failed, they failed fast.
  • Transosteal (transmandibular implant, TMI): through the bone. It penetrates both cortical plates and the full thickness of the alveolar bone. Problems: mandible only, anterior region only (because of the inferior alveolar nerve), extraoral incisions, excessive bone loss and general anesthesia.
ClassRelation to boneExamplesProblems
Endosteal (endosseous)In the bone; transects one cortical plateRoot form (most common), blade, ramus frameBlade and ramus frame: bone loss, high failure
Eposteal (subperiosteal)On the bone, under the periosteumSubperiosteal frameworkHard to retrieve, extensive surgery, bone loss
Transosteal (TMI)Through both cortical platesTransmandibular implantMandible and anterior only, extraoral incision, general anesthesia, bone loss

Healthy or failing?

"How do you diagnose a failing implant? And this will be definitely on your quiz or exam." The signs of failure on the slide: mobility, percussion pain, infection, radiolucency around the implant, and bone lost around it. Pain on function, especially deep bone pain or pain when tightening or loosening a component, is a bad sign; soreness of the mucosa alone is less worrying. Mobility means the implant is doomed. He walked through a health scale from success to failure:

GroupClinical picture
Success (optimum health)No pain or tenderness in function, no mobility, less than 2 mm of radiographic bone loss since surgery, no history of exudate
Satisfactory survivalNo pain, no mobility, 2-4 mm of bone loss, no history of exudate
Compromised survivalMay be sensitive, no mobility, more than 4 mm of bone loss but less than half the implant body, deeper pockets, may have exudate
FailureAny of: pain on function, mobility, bone loss more than half the length of the implant, uncontrolled exudate, or no longer in the mouth

Antibiotics help an implant with exudate, but they don't remove the bone loss or the pocket, so the problem comes back; the implant may need to be opened, cleaned and grafted, or the tissue repositioned and the exposed threads polished. The tissue around an implant is peri-implant mucosa, not gingiva, and its inflammation is peri-implant mucositis. Most important for you as the restorative dentist: take a radiograph before you start the crown, and don't take on the liability of restoring an implant that is already losing bone.

Causes of failure are multifactorial: the patient's medical history (tobacco, uncontrolled diabetes, genetics), overheating the bone during surgery (necrosis that never heals), implant movement during healing, maxilla vs mandible, peri-implantitis, functional overloading, and the patient's maintenance. Implants last a lifetime only if they are looked after.

Titanium

The ideal implant material is biocompatible, corrosion resistant, strong enough, increases osseointegration, easy to place, non-toxic and cost effective. Titanium is never found pure in nature; it is the ninth most abundant element in the earth's crust and very reactive. Its surface energy reacts with oxygen and spontaneously forms a tenacious, passivated titanium oxide layer, which reacts with osteoblasts to form calcium-phosphate apatite. That oxide is why titanium doesn't rust or corrode and is so biocompatible. It is a light, high-strength metal (golf clubs, racing bikes), which suits muscles that can bite harder than a thigh muscle pushes.

  • Commercially pure titanium (CP Ti): "commercially" because it can never be made fully pure; it always carries a little oxygen, nitrogen or iron. There are four grades (the slide ties them to the oxide), and strength rises with the grade. Modern implants use Grade IV.
  • Titanium alloy, Ti-6Al-4V (6% aluminum, 4% vanadium): the strongest.
  • The school's systems: BioHorizons is Ti-6Al-4V; Straumann and Nobel Biocare are Grade 4 CP titanium. Implants can fracture; if a patient breaks one, use a stronger implant (the alloy) next time.

Implant shape and surface

Early endosteal implants were smooth-surfaced cylinders tapped into place with a mallet; they are biomechanically less superior than machined, screw-type implants, which are threaded into a drilled osteotomy and give better primary stability, osseointegration and survival. Today's implants are screw-shaped (macro-topography) and carry a surface treatment (micro-topography) that creates surface microporosities, so osteoblasts settle into the valleys and integration is faster and more predictable. A textured surface is osteoconductive and integrates faster than a machined one; in the slide's graph, bone-to-implant contact was higher for treated surfaces than for machined ones in both jaws.

  • Additive treatments: titanium plasma spray (TPS), hydroxyapatite (HA) coating, microsphere bonding.
  • Subtractive treatments: acid etching, particle blasting.
  • The methods can be combined.

Each school system has its own surface ("this will also be on my exam"): Nobel Biocare TiUnite; Straumann SLA, sandblasted, large-grit, acid-etched (blasted with aluminum oxide grit, then acid-washed); BioHorizons RBT, resorbable blast texturing.

Why implants: the benefits

The interface half of the lecture starts with what implants do: they preserve bone volume (without an implant the anterior mandible keeps resorbing after extraction), preserve adjacent tooth structure (no need to prep neighbors for a bridge), and increase biting force and retention: "implant-retained removable prostheses generate more biting force compared to conventional prostheses," and mastication improves.

An implant is not a tooth

  • A tooth moves; an implant won't. An implant is like an ankylosed tooth with no periodontium.
  • Avoid splinting an implant to a tooth.
  • Don't place an implant in a patient who is still growing.
  • Avoid a cantilever on a single implant.
  • No connective tissue fibers attach to an implant's surface: only parallel and circular fibers.
  • The biologic width of a healthy implant averages 3.08 mm, about 1 mm greater than a healthy tooth's.

Because the implant has no periodontal ligament, it has no proprioception: the patient can't feel how hard they bite on it. So the implant crown or bridge gets light occlusal contact, adjusted with thin articulating paper (Accufilm) or shimstock. The biomechanics lecture takes this further.
readings.biomech:
What's tested
  • Wolff's law, stress and strain, and the adaptive window
  • Maxilla vs mandible: force distributing vs force absorbing, and Misch's D1-D4 bone
  • Compression, tension and shear: which bone tolerates best
  • Where implant treatment fails, and the patient and design factors behind it
  • Horizontal and vertical cantilevers, moment arms, and long spans
  • Bite force with different dentitions
  • Never connecting an implant to a tooth, and the goals of implant occlusion

Dr. Ramakiran Chavali's second lecture is built on Dr. Carl Misch's Contemporary Implant Dentistry. Mechanics is the branch of physics that deals with the action of force on bodies; applied to a biological system it is biomechanics. Just as a patient's smoking or uncontrolled diabetes changes implant outcomes, so do force factors, and you need them in mind every time you plan an implant.

Wolff's law

Wolff's law: the internal architecture of bone remodels according to the external forces (loads) applied. Trabeculae line up along the force trajectories, in the femur and in the jaws alike. When teeth are lost, chewing forces no longer reach the alveolar bone, and it resorbs year after year until only basal bone is left: a pencil-thin ridge under an old denture, or the mandibular canal lying on top of the ridge. The genial tubercles survive because the genioglossus and geniohyoid keep pulling on them. A maxillary molar with no opposing tooth shows sparse trabeculae next to one in function. Lose the tooth and you lose the bone, the keratinized tissue and the mucoperiosteum; an implant transmits force and preserves bone, so educate patients who say they don't want one.

Bone stays healthy inside an adaptive window. From less to more load: an acute disuse window (bone loss, disuse atrophy), the adapted window (balanced remodeling, healthy bone), mild overload (cells start to readapt), pathologic overload (microfractures) and finally spontaneous fracture. A missing, unreplaced tooth puts the bone in disuse; a well-planned implant puts it back in the adaptive zone; a badly designed prosthesis that magnifies force pushes it into overload, and the bone, implant or prosthesis fails.

Stress = force / area ("I want you to remember the stress is force per unit area"). Strain is deformation. Stress and strain are directly related.

Maxilla vs mandible

The maxilla has thin cortical plates and fine trabeculae; the mandible has thick cortical plates and a coarse trabecular pattern. The maxilla is a force distributing unit: it is full of cavities (sinuses, orbits, nasal cavity) and connects to the cranium, so a blow to the face crumples it before the force reaches the brain, like the crumple zone of a car. The mandible is a force absorbing unit: solid, thick bone made to take chewing loads. That is why implants fail more in the maxilla and succeed more in the mandible; warn a patient getting many maxillary implants, or one who has already lost one.

Misch bone classification

Misch divided jaw bone into four densities. Dr. Chavali asked you to write this down:

TypeDescriptionUsual location
D1Thick dense cortical bone, hardly any trabecular boneAnterior mandible
D2Thick cortical plates with coarse trabeculaePosterior mandible (sometimes anterior mandible)
D3Thin cortical plates, finer trabeculaeAnterior maxilla
D4Fine trabecular bone, very little cortical bone, more marrowPosterior maxilla

It's a generalization, not true in every patient. Density, strength, compressive strength and elastic modulus (stiffness) all fall from D1 to D4. A medical CT can measure density in Hounsfield units (Dr. Givan covers why CBCT values are unreliable), and an experienced surgeon can feel the bone type while drilling.

Forces on bone

Chewing loads bone in compression, tension (pulling) and shear (sliding, bending). Bone is strongest in compression, next in tension, and weakest in shear, so tensile and shear forces should be avoided on bone. He gave the question away: "Among the following forces, which is the most favorable to bone? ... compression. The least favorable would be shearing." Because the maxilla is proclined, maxillary implants often take more shear and tension than compression.

What fails, and why

An implant restoration has several interfaces: bone to implant, the implant's internal threads and the abutment screw, abutment to implant, and crown to abutment. Any of them can fail: the crown or porcelain can fracture, the screw can loosen (30 minutes to an hour to fix, hours if the head strips), the implant can fracture, or the bone can resorb and the osseointegration disappear. In Goodacre's review of complications:

ComplicationRate
Implants in the softest bone16%
Short implants17%
Overdenture attachment fracture or complications30%
Resin veneer fracture22%
Removable prosthesis fracture12%
Abutment or prosthetic screw loosening7-10%
Porcelain fracture7%
Prosthesis metal fracture3%
Implant fracture1-2%

Implants under 10 mm have tended to fail more. That isn't a contraindication (8 and 9 mm implants work well), but warn the patient when bone height near the nerve or sinus forces a short one. He then showed failures and their causes: a smooth cylindrical implant; an implant connected to natural teeth; bone loss under a cantilevered pontic; and a narrow implant under a huge molar crown, where the long moment arm resorbed the bone until the thin implant wall fractured. The fix there was a wider implant.

Sizing the implant to the tooth

The implant should complement the crown: you can't hang a big molar off a narrow implant. His general sizes: central incisor 3.5 mm, lateral incisor 3 mm, mandibular incisors 3 mm, premolars 3.5 or 4 mm, molars 4.5, 5 or 6 mm (4 mm or larger). The wax-up decides: mount casts, wax the ideal contours, make radiographic and surgical guides, and choose the size; a wide incisor may need 4 mm. The surgeon needs at least 1 mm of bone around the implant, so a 5 mm molar implant needs a 7 mm ridge. If the bone isn't there, the answer is to graft it, not to cheat with a narrower implant.

Where the forces come from: the patient

  • Age: generally, older patients generate lower masticatory force.
  • Gender: generally, men generate higher masticatory force than women.
  • Size and personality: generally, larger patients generate higher force. All of these are generalizations; some grandmothers can chew rocks.
  • Parafunction: bruxism and clenching generate higher force. Look for excessive tooth wear, fractures, abfractions, bony exostoses and absence of ideal occlusion. An occlusal splint (night guard) reduces the risk.
  • Tongue thrust: after teeth have been missing a long time the tongue can enlarge and push laterally.

When the biomechanical risk is high, the plan changes: increase the number of implants, use a reduced (smaller) occlusal table, and splint the implants together. A smaller crown shortens the moment arm; splinting spreads the force over a larger area, so stress (force/area) falls. The literature shows no difference in failure between splinted and unsplinted implants, but splint for a bruxer. Systemic factors (diabetes, smoking) are relative, not absolute, contraindications; osteoporosis usually doesn't cause failure, though bone-to-implant contact may be lower.

Mandibular flexure

The mandible flexes inward every time it opens. Implants on either side beyond the mental foramina should not be splinted together: tying anterior and posterior implants across the arch into one rigid prosthesis can cause pain and even fracture.

Prosthesis design

  • Always avoid cantilevering an implant prosthesis.
  • Avoid long-span implant-retained fixed partial dentures.
  • Always consider the opposing dentition.

Cantilevers

Both horizontal and vertical cantilevers are bad in implant dentistry and lead to complications and failures. Cantilevers are force magnifiers: moment of force = force x distance. The farther a load is from the implant (the fulcrum), the longer the moment arm and the bigger the force, like a diving board or pushing a door open near its knob rather than its hinge. His example: a 25 lb bite on a cantilevered pontic became 75 lb on the implant acting as the fulcrum and 50 lb on the other implant. The fix is another implant under the pontic (three implants for five units) or two separate bridges. The one exception he allowed: a cantilever may be acceptable when the opposing arch is a denture.

A vertical cantilever is a tall crown. As teeth, gums and bone are lost, the prosthesis must replace more than the crown, and gets longer, like a fence post that is easy to wiggle from the top. Misch's classification of fixed prostheses reflects this: FP-1 replaces the crown only, FP-2 the crown and part of the root, FP-3 crown, root, bone and soft tissue. To reduce a vertical cantilever, either do vertical ridge augmentation to get the ideal height back, or increase the number of implants to distribute the force. A pneumatized sinus calls for sinus grafting and more implants, not a long cantilever.

Span length

"As the length of the span increases by a unit, the flexibility increases by the cube": one unit flexes 1, two units 8, three units 27. A three-unit bridge on two implants is fine; a four-unit bridge on two implants usually isn't, unless the opposing arch is a denture or the patient bites lightly. For a heavy biter, three implants under a three-unit bridge. The implant, crown, cement and abutment screw all feel that flexing.

Opposing dentition and bite force

As teeth are lost, the proprioceptors in the periodontal ligament are lost with them, so forces in implant patients may be uncontrolled; implants opposing implants are the extreme case. The order of biting force:

Implant-supported FPD > natural dentition > implant-retained denture > complete denture

An opposing denture means the patient can't bite hard; opposing natural teeth mean more force and more implants.

Implant design

Smooth, cylindrical implants are biomechanically inferior to machined, screw-type implants, and the surface treatments (TiUnite, SLA, RBT) improve bone-to-implant contact further; threaded implants had significantly more contact than non-threaded ones. An external connection has a projection (a hex) sticking up from the implant; an internal connection has a receptacle inside with nothing sticking up. Most systems now use internal connections, and everything in the student clinic is internal; external designs are esthetically weaker. Titanium alloy is much stronger than commercially pure titanium.

Never connect an implant and a tooth

"This will be your exam question." Teeth are suspended in the periodontal ligament and can move apically about 25-100 microns; an implant can move only 3-5 microns, and that little comes from the viscoelasticity of bone. Join them and bite down: the tooth sinks into its ligament while the implant can't, so the implant takes the force, which leads to bone loss and failure. (In the fourth year you may hear of rare exceptions.)

Implant occlusion

"Occlusion, occlusion, occlusion." The implant crown should carry lighter contact than the adjacent teeth. Check the marks, then use shimstock, a very thin metal foil: it should hold on the natural teeth and pull through on the implant.

  • Single implant opposing a natural tooth: the natural tooth can move in function and accommodate the rigid implant crown. The implant crown is out of contact in MI when checked with shimstock; it may contact in forceful biting.
  • Two implant restorations opposing: the crowns are out of contact in forceful biting; shimstock drags but does not tear.
  • Direct occlusion along the long axis of the implant, with reduced cusp heights, a reduced occlusal table, and no interferences in excursive (eccentric) movements. Two premolar-sized crowns can be better than one huge molar.

This is the course director's own lecture (Dr. Chen), building on Dr. Chavali's introduction. It covers the terms you'll hear the moment you start restoring implants. The promise about the exam: "If you can totally understand what I have on the slide, you should have no problem. I don't ask you to study on the textbook."

1. Brands and product lines

Straumann, Nobel Biocare, BioHorizons and Zimmer are brands (companies). Each has several product lines, with different connections and platform sizes, and you need to know which one you're restoring; telling a company "a Nobel implant" isn't enough. You can't know every product on the market (about a hundred in the U.S. alone), but know the ones you use and the ones your surgeons use.

BrandProduct linesPlatformsAt school
Nobel BiocareConical Connection, Tri-LobeNP, RP, WPConical Connection
StraumannBone Level (CrossFit connection); synOcta (older, tissue level RN/WN)SC, NC, RC; RN, WNBone Level (NC or RC)
BioHorizonsTapered Internal, Tapered Internal Plus; new Tapered Pro Conical ("deep" conical, students starting to use it)3.0, 3.5, 4.5, 5.7 mmTapered Internal

2. Implant, abutment, screw, platform

The fixture is the implant. The platform is where the implant meets the abutment. Within one brand, the color of the implant platform and the abutment tells you which components match (Nobel's yellow is not BioHorizons' yellow). The wrong size or color of abutment or impression coping misfits: it can't seat all the way, or it spins.

Be careful with BioHorizons. The surgeon's note says "4.6 mm BioHorizons Tapered Internal Plus." If you pick the 4.5 mm (green) impression coping because the numbers are close, you're wrong: it needs the 3.5 mm (yellow) platform. The Plus line has extra platform switching, so its body diameter and platform differ. Worse, BioHorizons' hex lets the 4.5 mm part somewhat fit on the 4.6 mm implant, but the abutment is wider than the platform and the work has to be redone, at your cost. The surgeon cares about the body diameter; you care about the platform (the prosthetic connection). Find the implant's sticker in the surgeon's scanned chart (in Salud): it shows the platform. ("Stickers, stickers.") For Straumann, look at NC or RC (narrow or regular connection), not the 3.3, 4.1 or 4.8 mm body.

3. Platform switching

Platform switching (shifting) means the abutment diameter is smaller than the implant diameter. It moves the implant-abutment junction, the microgap, inward and away from the crestal bone, which preserves bone height, and it increases the soft tissue volume around the implant.

4. External vs internal connection

This is the way the abutment attaches to the implant. External: the female part is in the abutment (the implant has a hex sticking up). Internal: the female part is in the implant.

ExternalInternal
More force on the abutment and screw: higher chance of screw looseningMore force on the implant itself
Higher tolerance of implant divergence when splintedLess microgap between implant and abutment under force

All the implants used at school have an internal connection.

5. Bone level vs tissue level

This is where the implant's platform sits. A tissue-level implant has a smooth, polished collar that sits above the bone, in the soft tissue, with the rough surface below it covered by bone; a bone-level implant's platform sits at the bone. Tissue level puts the microgap away from the bone, potentially less bone loss. Bone level gives more room to contour the emergence profile, potentially better esthetics: the tissue-level collar already takes about a millimeter, leaving about 2 mm to shape the crown out of the tissue instead of 3.

6. Parallel-walled vs tapered

This is the implant's shape. A parallel-walled implant has more surface area contacting bone. A tapered implant has higher primary stability (greater lateral compression of the bone during insertion) and less chance of hitting neighboring structures such as a root or nerve.

7. Primary and secondary stability

Primary + secondary stability = total stability. When the implant is placed, primary stability locks it in; it is measured as insertion torque in Ncm. As the bone remodels, primary stability falls and secondary stability gradually rises, until new bone holds the implant. The transition causes a stability dip, weeks after placement; when exactly depends on the brand and its surface treatment. If the surgeon allows it (there is enough primary stability), you can work on the implant right after surgery, for example to make a provisional; after that, be cautious about touching the implant until the total stability recovers. (In the lecture he said he feels comfortable at about 6-8 weeks, but follows the surgeon, who may say 3 months.)

8. Torque and torque wrenches

Torque is rotational friction: between the implant and the bone during insertion, or between screw and thread when tightening a screw. Use a torque wrench (beam type or toggle type) to apply precise torque; your fingers apply only about 5 Ncm. The screw has to be tight enough not to loosen, yet still removable if the crown has to come off. The general rules for implant screws, "the common numbers you will need to memorize":

SystemTorque
Nobel Biocare35 Ncm (the 3.0 mm implant: 15 Ncm)
Straumann35 Ncm
BioHorizons30 Ncm

Numbers are company- and product-specific (angled screw channels can differ). Don't torque on a printed model.

9. Conical connection and Morse taper

A conical connection is a type of internal connection in which the abutment has a tapered surface where it contacts the implant. Compared with internal non-conical connections, there is no significant difference in implant survival or biological complications, but the conical connection has less microgap at the junction (slope against slope), so less marginal bone loss and fewer prosthetic complications. Nobel's examples: its internal connection has a 45-degree shallow cone, its CONELOG a 7.5-degree deep cone. A Morse taper is a taper that causes "cold welding" (friction) between implant and abutment: a type of conical connection, at specific degrees of taper (Straumann synOcta; Dentsply Sirona Ankylos at 5.7 degrees). Whether a company's taper is a "true" Morse taper matters less than knowing it's conical.

10. Cover screw vs healing abutment

A cover screw is used at the first stage of a two-stage surgery: it's short and hidden under the soft tissue, for example when the implant isn't stable enough to be exposed to the tongue and food. A healing abutment is taller and is not covered by the tissue: it's used in one-stage surgery or at the second stage of a two-stage surgery, and it comes in different heights and widths. The sequence: implants placed, cover screws attached, primary closure; then uncovering, and healing abutments attached.

11. Ideal implant position

"These are the numbers you must remember."

  • Depth: the platform 3-4 mm below the ideal buccal gingival margin (copy the margin from the proximal tooth). About 3 mm is the implant's biologic width, and the extra gives room to grow the emergence profile from the narrow implant to the crown's width.
  • Proximal: 1.5 mm from a natural tooth (for the bone's blood supply, and to stay off the PDL), and 3 mm between two implants.
  • Why at least 3 mm between implants: extra bone resorbs between them, compromising the soft tissue height, so the papilla is lost (black triangles, exposed threads).
  • Facial, especially for anterior teeth and immediate placement: 2 mm from the border of the bone, because the buccal bundle bone always resorbs after extraction.
  • Lingual: at least 1 mm from the border of the bone.
  • Anterior implants are generally placed lingually (palatally): it makes a screw-retained design possible and avoids esthetic problems. A grayish color in the buccal tissue over an implant can mean there's no bone covering it.
  • Posterior implants are generally at the middle of the ridge (over the central fossa), where the bone is easier to maintain, at least 1 mm from the buccal and lingual borders. If the bone isn't wide enough: ridge augmentation.

12. Engaging vs non-engaging abutments

An engaging abutment engages the implant's anti-rotation feature (a hex, octagon or grooves) and cannot spin once fully seated. Straumann RC uses 4 grooves; BioHorizons a hex. A non-engaging abutment can spin freely even when fully seated; its connection part is shorter.

13. Impression copings

An impression coping screws onto the implant to transfer its position, deep in the bone under the soft tissue, to the cast. The student clinic uses a closed-tray coping 99% of the time (and the PCD project practices only closed tray), but for multiple units an open-tray impression is more accurate, because the coping is unscrewed and comes out inside the impression instead of being removed and reinserted.

14. Screw-retained vs cement-retained

Screw-retained: abutment and crown are assembled as one piece, and the screw channel penetrates the crown. Cement-retained: abutment and crown are separate; the abutment is screwed in and the crown is cemented on it in the mouth, so no screw channel shows on the crown. Screws are used in both designs.

Screw-retainedCement-retained
Retrievable: crown and abutment come out through the screw channelMore passive connection between implant and abutment (especially for an FPD)
No residual cement issueNo screw channel on the crown: more esthetic, higher crown strength

If the implant position lets the screw channel come out on the lingual of an anterior crown, screw-retained is doable (you can still cement if you prefer). If the implant is too facial, the channel would perforate the incisal edge or even the facial, so cement-retained is indicated.

A conventional screw-retained crown is a true one-piece structure: metal cast onto the platform and porcelain fired on the metal. Today there's also the screwmentable crown: a custom abutment or TiBase plus a full-ceramic crown with a screw channel, bonded together with permanent (resin) cement outside the mouth, keeping the channel. It is a "fake one-piece."

If you really want screw retention on a facial implant, there are angled screw channels: Nobel Biocare's ASC, BioHorizons' Precision Angled Screw, Straumann's Angled Solutions (AS). They need a special screwdriver and screw (every brand different), cost a higher lab fee, may loosen more than conventional screws (in vitro), and beyond about 15 degrees of correction the chance of stripping the screw rises.

15. Prefabricated vs custom abutments

Prefabricated abutments come from the manufacturer in specific heights and sizes; some can be slightly adjusted (only by cutting away). Examples: TiBase (Variobase), solid abutments, anatomic abutments. Custom abutments have their whole contour designed for the patient (the final crown and the soft tissue): Straumann CARES milled abutments, or a castable (UCLA) abutment.

PrefabricatedCustom
Generally straight contour with a uniform marginMaximizes retention and resistance form for the crown
Sometimes needs adjustment to fit the patient (subtractive only)Traces the soft tissue contour: less chance of an extremely deep margin that interferes with cement cleanup

Custom abutments are generally always engaging: a contoured abutment that could spin would never sit the same way twice. A TiBase is short; he showed a crown that separated from one after a year.

Which abutment for which restoration

  • Single crown: the abutment must be engaging, whether screw- or cement-retained, or the crown will spin. A prefabricated TiBase (screwmentable) or a custom abutment (screwmentable or cement-retained) are both acceptable.
  • Cement-retained FPD: custom abutments (so the cement can be cleaned up), and they must be engaging; if anatomic abutments could spin, the bridge couldn't be seated. A TiBase is for screw-retained only.
  • Screw-retained FPD: ideally non-engaging. The splinted one-piece bridge can't spin on the implants anyway, and since two implants are almost never perfectly parallel, the longer engaging connection would bind on insertion and put more force on the implants.
  • But the original manufacturers (Straumann, BioHorizons) offer only engaging single custom abutments. A castable (PFM) design can be made non-engaging; for zirconia they'll have you use a non-engaging TiBase (Variobase).

In the student clinic: single crown, always engaging. FPD cement-retained: custom abutments, engaging. FPD screw-retained: TiBase, non-engaging. And follow your faculty's choice of cement- or screw-retained.

16. Interocclusal space

Every implant prosthesis needs enough space between the bone or implant platform and the opposing tooth, and how much depends on its design. Extremely limited space makes any restoration hard.

  • Cement-retained: a margin more than 1 mm subgingival can leave uncleanable cement, leading to peri-implantitis and bone loss. You still need resistance and retention form (an abutment 3-4 mm tall), the crown's thickness (1 mm for zirconia), and the implant's biologic width of about 3 mm. For a molar: 3 (biologic width) - 1 (subgingival) + 4 (abutment) + 1 (crown) = 7 mm minimum, from the bone to the opposing tooth.
  • Screw-retained, castable (true one-piece): about 4 mm from the platform for the collar, the screw head and the material sealing the channel; so it can sit only 1 mm above the soft tissue if there's no porcelain on top (4 mm minus the 3 mm biologic width), like a partially erupted tooth. Possible, but hard to keep clean.
  • Screwmentable: a subgingival margin isn't a concern, because the cement is removed outside the mouth. 1 mm from the platform to the abutment margin + 4 mm of abutment for retention + 1-2 mm of zirconia = 6-7 mm from the platform, or 3-4 mm above the soft tissue. TiBases come in 1-4 mm heights.

17. Crown-to-implant ratio

There is more forgiveness on the crown-to-implant ratio than on a natural tooth's crown-to-root ratio (1:1), because an implant behaves like an ankylosed tooth with no PDL. But a larger ratio (a 15 mm crown, about 2:1) may bring more prosthetic complications (screw loosening, fracture) or marginal bone loss from unfavorable force distribution; consider splinting the implants.

18. Emergence profile and the E, B and C zones

The emergence profile (not "emergency profile") is the contour of the implant restoration, controlled by the abutment or the crown, between the implant platform and the soft tissue margin. Starting at the platform:

  • C zone: the first 1-1.5 mm; kept straight, for the blood supply of the connective tissue and for bone remodeling. It's determined by the abutment.
  • B zone: between C and E; variable, but concave is preferred, to keep tissue volume. It's the "running room."
  • E zone: the last 1 mm under the gingival margin; directly related to how the crown and gingiva look. It's determined by esthetics and extends from the cervical of the wax-up.

Other authors call the E zone the critical contour (convex most of the time) and the B and C zones together the subcritical contour (straight to concave). The rules: to make the gingival margin creep down (coronally), or if the implant is placed more buccally, make the E zone (even the B zone) more concave. To move the margin up (apically), or if the implant is more lingual, make it more convex. On the palatal side, follow the natural tooth contour. You'll practice this in the lab.

19. Teflon (PTFE) tape

Plumber's tape, made to seal pipe threads, is now the popular material for sealing the screw channel (it used to be gutta percha, PVS or a cotton pellet). Pack it densely into the channel, leaving about 2 mm, then add packable composite on top. The composite must never touch the screw head, or the screw is no longer retrievable; and cement must not run into the channel either.

20. Verification index (jig)

For a splinted implant FPD, a verification index confirms that the implants' relationship on the cast matches the mouth, because every impression carries some error, and an implant bridge is far less forgiving than a tooth-borne bridge (no PDL). After the PVS impression is poured, splinted resin indexes are made on the cast, bound to non-engaging temporary abutments (an engaging part might bind and hide a misfit). The index is sectioned, re-splinted with resin in the mouth (the intraoral relationship is the most accurate), and taken back to the cast, where it must passively reseat on the analogs. The lab technician can help. (A non-engaging index checks position, not rotation.)

Two ways to check that a framework fits passively: the one-screw test (Sheffield test): tighten only the screw at the far end and watch whether the other abutments lift; and tactile sense: tighten several screws gently and slowly, and extra resistance on one means it isn't passive.

21. Placement and loading timeline (ITI 2018)

TermTiming
Immediate placementSame day as the extraction
Early placementWith soft tissue healing (4-8 weeks) or partial bone healing (12-16 weeks) after extraction
Late placementAfter complete bone healing, more than 6 months after extraction
Immediate loadingWithin 1 week of implant placement
Early loadingBetween 1 week and 2 months after placement
Conventional loadingMore than 2 months of healing, with no prosthesis connected

The consensus graded each combination: conventional loading is scientifically and clinically valid after immediate, early or late placement; late placement with early loading is valid too; immediate placement with immediate or early loading, and late placement with immediate loading, are clinically documented; early placement with immediate or early loading has insufficient documentation. Follow your surgeon's decision. And note: immediately attaching a provisional (immediate restoration or provisionalization) does not mean you have to put it under function (immediate loading). If there's no need to load it, don't load it immediately.

The ITI's criteria for immediate restoration or loading:

  • Intact socket walls
  • A facial bone wall at least 1 mm thick
  • Thick soft tissue
  • No acute infection at the site
  • Bone apical and lingual to the socket, to provide primary stability
  • Insertion torque of 25-40 Ncm and/or an ISQ above 70
  • An occlusal scheme that protects the provisional during function
  • Patient compliance

22. Anodizing titanium

Anodizing changes a titanium abutment's color by controlling the thickness of its oxide layer in an electrolytic bath at a specific voltage (about 65 volts for gold, about 75 for pink). The layer is under a micron thick, so it doesn't affect the fit, and grinding removes the color.
