readings.prefab:
What's tested
  • Prefabricated (stock) vs custom abutments: pros, cons, and when each is used
  • The abutments used during and after surgery: cover screw, healing abutment, temporary and final abutments
  • One-stage vs two-stage surgery, and who should get which
  • Engaging vs non-engaging temporary abutments
  • UCLA (cast) vs CAD/CAM custom abutments
  • Cement-retained vs screw-retained, the 5 mm rule, and peri-implantitis risk
  • What the lab needs from you

In this recorded lecture Dr. Chavali covers prefabricated abutments, the stock parts made by the manufacturer that fit any patient, and briefly one kind of custom abutment, the UCLA abutment. Dr. Arce covers custom abutments in more depth. In the PCD lab your last exercise is preparing a prefabricated abutment, and you'll see a demonstration of a custom one (you make its Regisil mockup). He flagged several exam questions as he went.

Two classes of abutments

Prefabricated abutments, also called stock abutments, are already manufactured: take one off the shelf and use it on any patient, one size fits all. Custom abutments are made for one patient. Prefabricated abutments have real shortfalls, which is why the clinic almost always uses custom ones.

Abutments by stage

His own way of sorting them (not from the literature):

  • During surgery (pre-prosthetic): the cover screw and the healing abutment.
  • Temporary abutments: prosthetic abutments that can go on at the time of surgery, for a cement-retained or screw-retained provisional.
  • Final abutments: prefabricated final abutments, or custom abutments: the cast UCLA, or a CAD/CAM milled abutment.

One-stage and two-stage surgery

In two-stage surgery the surgeon opens a flap, places the implant, puts on a cover screw and closes everything. A few months later the flap is reopened, the cover screw removed and a healing abutment placed, with the tissue sutured around it so it sticks out: the implant is now open (patent) to the mouth. It takes about three weeks for the tissue to heal around the healing abutment, and then you're ready for the final crown. In one-stage surgery there is no cover screw: the healing abutment goes on at placement and the tissue closes around it, so there's no second surgery.

Choosing between them is an important decision. For diabetics and smokers, "you don't want to take any chance": close it up and let the implant heal completely, not open to the mouth. For a young, healthy patient with no medical history, no parafunctional habits and no heavy forces, one-stage is reasonable.

Healing abutments

Healing abutments come in different heights, widths and emergence profiles. The soft tissue height above the implant varies from patient to patient (much of it is genetic): use a 1 mm healing abutment if the implant is very superficial, a much taller one if it's submerged deep. The profile shapes the tissue for the final crown: incisors get a straight (narrow) profile, and molars and wide premolars get a wide one, so the tissue heals into a diverging cuff; there's also a regular profile in between.

Temporary abutments

Temporary abutments are titanium and come screw-retained (titanium cylinders with notches) or cement-retained (with a plastic cap or sleeve on top to cement the provisional to). For a cement-retained provisional: seat the abutment, snap the sleeve on, reduce it for occlusal clearance, fill a vacuform matrix with Jet acrylic, seat it so the sleeve is picked up and bonds to the acrylic, trim the excess and cement with temporary cement. A short conical cement-retained abutment suits molars or tight occlusal clearance; a tall titanium cylinder suits cases that need height.

Temporary abutments can be engaging, with a hex (a protuberance) that locks into the implant, or non-engaging, smooth and converging. The non-engaging screw-retained abutment is the one used for a bridge.

The screw-retained provisional has the advantage of no excess cement. Cement that escapes under an implant restoration acts like calculus and causes gingival inflammation, peri-implant mucositis and peri-implantitis. For an immediate screw-retained provisional, the titanium cylinder is placed, picked up in the Jet acrylic, finished outside the mouth, screwed back in and the screw hole closed with composite. Once the tissue architecture is formed, the final impression is taken.

The prefabricated abutment

A prefabricated final abutment is prepared like a crown-and-bridge tooth, for example with a chamfer margin, on the implant analog in the stone model; the crown is made on it, the abutment seated in the mouth, its screw hole blocked with Teflon tape and a resin, and the crown cemented.

Prefabricated (stock)Custom
FitVery precise: same manufacturer, same milling, tight tolerancesPrecise too: originals milled by the manufacturer or under its patents
CostCheap: about $50 from the manufacturer, sometimes free (BioHorizons)About $150-200 from a lab
StrengthSaid to be highHigh
PreparationMust be modified (margins dropped, prepared like a tooth)Designed to fit; little or no prep
MarginCan end up deep under the tissue if the implant is deep, trapping cementPlaced where you want, near or above the gum line: cement cleans up
Emergence profileThin "thimble" under a wide molar: poorExcellent; looks like a customized crown prep

The big disadvantage of a prefabricated abutment: if the implant is placed deep and no abutment is tall enough, its margin sits far below the gum, cement gets trapped, and no scalpel or sickle scaler can reach it, leading to peri-implantitis. A margin at or slightly above the gingiva (epigingival) is fine.

Prefabricated abutments come in different cuff heights (1, 2, 3 and even 5 mm). Measure the soft tissue height by removing the healing abutment and probing from the implant collar to the deepest point of the gum, or on a soft tissue model, and choose the cuff height so the margin isn't too deep; a deep implant can't use a 1 mm cuff. They also come straight or angled: a malpositioned (off-center or misangled) implant needs an angled prefabricated abutment or a custom one. An implant placed far to the facial can't take a screw-retained crown, because the hole would show every time the patient smiles; it needs a cement-retained crown on an angled prefabricated or a custom abutment, which can pull the angulation back.

In the second-floor clinic, "99.9% of the time you're going to do a custom abutment."

Custom abutments: UCLA vs CAD/CAM

The UCLA abutment (University of California, Los Angeles) is a plastic sleeve on a titanium base, in diameters specific to each system. The lab cuts it down, adds wax to shape it, sprues it, invests it (gypsum-bonded, ethyl silicate or phosphate-bonded investment), burns it out and casts it: a cast custom abutment. A CAD/CAM custom abutment is designed on a computer from a scan and milled: the newer approach.

Cement-retained vs screw-retained

Either abutment, prefabricated or custom, can carry a cement-retained or a screw-retained crown. Cement-retained: screw in the abutment, cement the crown. Screw-retained: abutment and crown are one unit, screwed in through a hole in the crown.

  • Esthetics: cement-retained is often more esthetic, especially when the implant emerges toward the facial; screw-retained can be less esthetic.
  • Peri-implantitis: the risk is much higher with cement-retained crowns; none with screw-retained, because no cement is used. (An exam question.)
  • Biomechanics: screw-retained can be less favorable if the implant isn't along the long axis, wasn't placed with a guide, or is malpositioned.
  • Space: a cement-retained crown needs a minimum of 5 mm of occlusal (interocclusal) clearance.

"This is an exam question": if the interocclusal space is 5 mm or less, you must do screw-retained; you have no choice. Above 5 mm you can do either, unless the implant emerges so far facially that the access hole would come through the facial or buccal and show; then you must use cement-retained.

The numbers in the other lectures count from a different starting point: the terminology lecture's 7 mm for a cement-retained molar runs from the bone (including about 3 mm of biologic width), and Dr. Geisinger's table gives 7-8 mm for cement-retained and 7.5 mm for screw-retained crowns and bridges. Dr. Chavali's 5 mm is the clearance he asks you to check on the mounted casts; when a question names his rule, the answer is 5 mm.

What the lab needs

Another exam question: what you have to send the lab so they can make the abutment and crown.

  • Mounted casts, with a soft tissue model (the pink material around the analog).
  • The implant system: Nobel, Straumann or BioHorizons, and the product line.
  • The diameter (3, 3.5, 4, 4.3, 5 mm...).
  • The soft tissue height, which the soft tissue model gives you.
  • A completed implant order form from the second-floor clinic.

Know the three systems (another example question): BioHorizons (3, 3.5 and 4 mm; the school uses its internal connection), Nobel Biocare (regular and narrow collars; conical connection, tri-lobe and external lines; the school uses the conical connection), and Straumann (tissue level and bone level; the school uses bone level). Implant analogs are color-coded by diameter.

The multi-unit abutment used for All-on-4 cases is beyond the undergraduate level.
readings.imaging:
What's tested
  • Dr. Givan's study guide: the uses of imaging in the three phases of implant treatment
  • The three most common imaging modalities for implants, and ALARA
  • Advantages and disadvantages of periapical and panoramic images
  • Medical CT vs cone beam CT; the Hounsfield scale
  • Advantages and problems of CT scans, and their artifacts
  • Scan templates and prosthetically driven planning; implant planning software

Dr. Daniel Givan (Restorative Sciences) gave this as the first half of one session; the second half, the basic science of CBCT, is the next lecture. "It would be nearly impossible to do implantology without the help of imaging": imaging shows what's happening at the crest, within the trabecular bone, where the implant sits and in the supporting structures. His hint for the exam, from the course: be able to answer the details on his study guide ("what do I want you to know"). This lecture covers its first ten items.

Prosthetically driven, biologically balanced

Implants are placed for a purpose: "not because the patient is suffering from titanium insufficiency." The patient wants teeth, so what matters is the prosthesis (an implant crown, an implant denture), and the implant exists to support it. That's why implant planning is a prosthetically driven but biologically balanced process: you can plan the prosthesis however you like, but without supporting structures to put the implant into, it won't work. You need to know where the teeth must be, how they'll be supported, and how to place the implant without violating sensitive structures (the inferior alveolar nerve, a site with no blood supply), and esthetics drives much of it too.

Imaging in the three phases of treatment

  • Phase 1, pre-surgical: determine the quality, quantity and angulation of bone; locate critical structures relative to the proposed implant sites; determine whether disease is present at those sites.
  • Phase 2, surgical and interoperative: evaluate the sites during and immediately after surgery; assist the optimal position and orientation of the implants; evaluate the healing and integration phase; make sure the abutment position and prosthesis fabrication are correct.
  • Phase 3, post-prosthetic: begins once the prosthesis is placed and lasts as long as the implants remain; evaluates long-term maintenance of rigid fixation and function, including the crestal bone level and the implant complex. The crest is the early warning sign that an implant may be lost.

Modalities

The options include periapical, panoramic, occlusal and cephalometric radiography, tomography (including CBCT), computed tomography, MRI and interactive CT. The three most common for implant therapy are periapical, panoramic and cone beam CT. The guiding principle when choosing: ALARA, "as low as reasonably achievable" dose.

A CBCT is roughly three times a panoramic image and about a tenth of a medical CT. Be skeptical of manufacturers' dose figures (a pan at 26 microsieverts, a full-mouth series at 150, a medical CT at 1,200-3,300, and some CBCTs quoted very low): they leave out the scout images, positioning and the size of the area scanned, so real CBCT doses are generally higher than the vendors say.

Periapical images

"Intra-oral radiographs can be very accurate when taken with extreme care."

  • Advantages: very high resolution.
  • Disadvantages: no bone width; no quantitative bone quality; magnification and distortion (from angulation errors).

PAs and bitewings are by far the number one go-to for monitoring implants: take them at baseline and follow them routinely, looking at the crest for bone right against the implant or a defect starting. A standard PA works for planning and placement; for following bone levels during maintenance, a bitewing-style film parallel to the crest is best.

Panoramic images

The panoramic image is the most common image in dentistry. It shows the overall status of the teeth and supporting bone, anatomical anomalies and pathology, and sorts sites into those where implants will be straightforward, those that need grafting or distraction, and those where implants aren't advisable. It's an excellent screening tool, with terrible superimposition, distortion and magnification.

  • Reddy et al. 1994: errors as large as 30% in estimating bone height from panoramic films, and bone width cannot be estimated at all.
  • Advantages: a very good overview.
  • Disadvantages: no bone width; no quantitative bone quality; variable magnification; patient positioning is crucial.
  • Measuring through the magnification: put ball bearings of known diameter (usually 4-5 mm) in a radiographic template, measure them on the pan and get the magnification (distortion) ratio. It's valid only vertically, and only in the area of the focus.

To assess bone width you need cross-sectional imaging. A pan's focal trough is wide, about 8-15 mm; a panoramic slice from a CBCT is about a millimeter thick, with cross-sections through it.

Tomography

A tomogram is a two-dimensional image of a slice or section through a three-dimensional object. In conventional tomography (tomography by blurring), the x-ray source moves one way while the film moves the opposite way during the exposure, so structures in the focal plane stay sharp and those in other planes blur. The tomogram is the picture, the tomograph the apparatus, and tomography the process.

Medical CT vs cone beam CT

Medical CTCone beam CT
BeamFan beamCone-shaped beam from the source to a flat panel
RotationVery rapidRelatively slow
DataA helix or spiral, interpolated into a set of slices2-D projections reconstructed into a 3-D volume (needs significant computing power)
VolumeLarge anatomical regions very quicklyA medium-sized volume in a single rotation
Patient positionSupine: claustrophobic, soft tissues collapse, TMJ not in its natural positionSitting up (or standing): more comfortable
DoseHigherLower (5x to 10x less)
ContrastBetter soft tissue contrastMore Compton scatter, so less soft tissue contrast

Early cone beams were supine too, but makers soon realized that, like a pan, they work with the patient sitting or standing. They cost roughly $75,000 to $250,000.

The Hounsfield scale

"________ ________ scale is a measure of radiodensity": the Hounsfield unit scale, named for the founder of CT. For quantitative measurement of bone density, relative radiodensity is correlated to known tissue densities and measured in Hounsfield units. The values are hoped to relate to the primary stability an implant will get, but current evidence does not support that. (The study guide asks you to know this definition and the slightly different one in the next lecture: HU describe a voxel's attenuation relative to air and water.)

Advantages of a CT scan

  • Accurate length measurements: bone width, height and depth (within about 0.1-0.5 mm in all three directions, so you can plan safety zones around the nerve and neighboring teeth).
  • Freedom from geometric distortion.
  • Quantitative assessment of bone quality: profiles and histograms (though with CBCT it's mostly qualitative).
  • Models and drill guides.
  • Diagnostic quality images.
  • The possibility of flapless surgery: if you know exactly where the implant goes, you can punch through the tissue without a flap. Possible, though not done much.

Problems with CT scans

  • Remove dentures or other fixtures with metal clasps, reinforcements or chrome-cobalt bases before scanning.
  • Some suggest replacing amalgam with composite if the tooth will be sacrificed anyway (an ethical question).
  • Metal restorations scatter the beam (Compton scatter) and make the image hard to read; zirconia is less of a problem.
  • Patient movement during the scan blurs the image.

Artifacts

  • Motion artifact: the patient or the scan template moves during scanning (a dark gap between template and tissue gives it away).
  • Starburst artifact: arises when there are sharp changes in density, between air and bone or between bone and dense metal. It's caused by limits in high-frequency sampling, not by scattered radiation.
  • Beam hardening: occurs when metals are present; metals filter the low-energy x-rays out of the beam, so parts of the image appear black.
  • Titanium implants produce little artifact, while gold produces a lot.

Scan templates

The study guide's freebie: a scan template is a temporary prosthesis, worn during the CT scan, that replaces the missing teeth so they show up in the volumetric image, letting you see the proposed teeth in 3-D against the existing bone. It gives rise to the theme of treatment planning: prosthetically driven implant planning and surgery. If you know where the proposed restorations will be, the implant support can be planned. The template:

  • Provides inter-arch stability and holds the position relationship during the scan.
  • Opens the vertical dimension slightly (a few mm), which improves the imaging of the teeth.
  • Lets you see the orientation and dimensions of the proposed restoration in the CT images (for example with gutta percha markers on the denture teeth or wax-up).

Next year this is balanced with biology: the plan must fit the existing structures, or the ability to augment them.

The process

  1. Planning: fabricate a radiographic guide; scan the patient; plan in the software.
  2. Optional guided surgery: fabricate the surgical guide from the digital plan; complete guided surgery. A drill guide may rest on bone, mucosa or teeth, and a sleeve in the guide directs the drill's position, orientation and depth.

Implant planning software

In interactive planning software, implants are added virtually into the CBCT image and viewed three-dimensionally. Examples: Simplant (Dentsply Sirona/Materialise), Implant Design Studio (3Shape), Nobel Clinician (Nobel Biocare), coDiagnostiX (DWOS/Straumann), Invivo (Anatomage) and Blue Sky Bio. Views include the panoramic slice and its cross-sections, plus sagittal and coronal views; which ones a clinician uses depends on their training.
readings.cbct:
What's tested
  • Dr. Givan's study guide, items 11-19: what CBCT stands for and how it operates
  • The x-ray source: kVp, thermionic emission, characteristic and Bremsstrahlung x-rays, a polyenergetic beam, filters and collimators
  • Attenuation and the four interactions of x-rays with tissue (and the two that matter most)
  • Digital receptors: computed radiography vs indirect flat-panel detectors; pixels, resolution, signal-to-noise and dynamic range
  • ROI, FoV and ALARA
  • Processing: basis images, reconstruction, voxels, DICOM, the views
  • Artifacts: scatter, beam hardening, motion; and why Hounsfield units are unreliable in CBCT

After the break Dr. Givan went back to basic science: how x-rays are made, how they pass through tissue and how a cone beam turns them into a volume. He admitted it's tough material, but it explains two things you'll fight with every day: why imaging is hard around metal (most of your patients' mouths) and why some numbers on a CBCT can't be trusted. Modern CBCT came to dentistry in the late 1990s. Most dental use of CBCT software is virtual planning, with a small but growing share for guided surgery.

Radiation principles

"Medical imaging has come to represent the largest man-made source of ionizing radiation in developed countries." Hence ALARA, a dose "as low as reasonably achievable"; a field of view limited to the area of interest; and shielding, collimation and other safety steps.

How a CBCT works

CBCT stands for cone beam computed tomography. In 3-4 sentences, the study guide's summary:

  • An x-ray source and a detector are mounted on a rotating gantry (the frame that holds them), with the patient positioned in the axis of rotation.
  • A cone- or pyramid-shaped x-ray beam is directed through the patient's region of interest (ROI).
  • In a single 180 or 360 degree rotation, a series of sequential planar images is captured (usually several hundred).
  • The planar images are combined by algorithms into a volume, which can be viewed in the three orthogonal planes (axial, sagittal, coronal), in multiplanar views or as a 3-D iso-surface.

Remember: in tomography the source and detector rotate around the patient, who can be supine, sitting or standing. The imaging chain runs from the source (generates x-rays), through the patient (x-rays are attenuated), to the detector (receives what's left and converts it to a digital signal).

The source

The x-ray tube is a vacuum tube with a cathode and an anode. A voltage is applied across them, measured as the peak kilovoltage (kVp). The cathode filament is heated until it emits electrons: thermionic emission. The electrons fly to the anode and strike its focal spot (about 0.5 mm, made of tungsten; the spot's size affects sharpness) at high velocity. About 99% of their energy becomes heat and only about 1% becomes x-ray photons. The anode is tilted to aim the x-rays at the tube's exit window.

kVp and energy: the voltage sets how much kinetic energy the electrons gain, so higher kVp means higher-energy x-rays. Higher-energy ("hard") photons are less affected by attenuation, penetrate more and suit dense or thick tissue: they're the ones wanted for medical imaging (and airport security). Low-energy ("soft") x-rays, used for mammography and crystallography, are filtered out in CBCT. What kind of x-ray comes out depends on the focal spot material and the energy of the striking electron.

Two ways x-rays are made

  • Characteristic x-rays: most electrons miss the tungsten atoms and just make heat, but about 1% knock out an inner-shell (K-shell) electron. An outer-shell electron drops in to fill the vacancy and releases the difference in binding energy as a photon of a very specific energy (the K and L lines).
  • Bremsstrahlung ("braking") x-rays: electrons passing near a tungsten nucleus are slowed and redirected by its pull, and the lost energy leaves as an x-ray. The energy varies with how close the electron passes.

So the overall beam is polyenergetic: it contains photons of varying energies in a continuous spectrum.

Filtering

X-rays leave the anode in all directions, and only those reaching the exit window leave the tube. The window is covered by the primary filter, usually aluminum or copper (2.5-10 mm), which absorbs the low-energy photons; those would otherwise be absorbed by the patient's tissue and only add dose (more damage). The beam is then delimited by rectangular collimator plates of lead alloy. To cut exposure further, the tube is pulsed in step with the detector, which can reduce exposure time by up to 50% (so the exposure time is shorter than the scan time); the tube current (mA) and kVp can also be controlled.

Attenuation

As the beam passes through the body, internal structures absorb or scatter part of it, and the rest reaches the detector to make the image. Attenuation is the reduction of the intensity of an x-ray beam as it traverses matter, by absorption and/or deflection (scatter) of photons. It depends on the beam's energy, the number of photons, and the density and atomic number of the absorber:

  • The thicker the material, the greater the attenuation (thick bone vs thin).
  • The higher the atomic number and/or density, the greater the attenuation. Gold (atomic number 79, density 19.32 g/cm³) scatters a lot around gold restorations; titanium (atomic number 22, 4.43 g/cm³) scatters little.

Four interactions with tissue

  1. No interaction: the photon passes straight through to the detector; that area looks radiolucent.
  2. Absorption: the photoelectric effect. The photon gives up all its energy colliding with an atom and ejects a K-shell electron, leaving an ion; this is why x-rays are ionizing radiation. Its probability rises with atomic number (why lead, atomic number 82, shields) and falls as photon energy rises (why high-energy beams penetrate).
  3. Rayleigh scattering (also called Thomson, coherent or classical scattering): the photon interacts with the whole atom and changes direction without changing energy. It increases with atomic number but is a minor contributor.
  4. Compton scattering: the photon is deflected by an electron, which gains energy and is ejected; the photon loses energy and travels on along a new path with a longer wavelength. If it's detected and reconstructed, it appears as an artifact. Compton scatter is the main difference between CBCT and medical CT images.

The two most important are absorption (photoelectric) and Compton scattering.

Receptors

Film was the original (analog) receptor. There are two kinds of digital receptors:

  • Computed radiography (CR): phosphor plates sensitive to x-rays capture a latent image, a laser scanner reads it out to digital, and the plate is erased for reuse. UAB uses phosphor plates for its periapicals and bitewings. CR is not used for CBCT.
  • Direct radiography (DR): x-rays are converted directly or indirectly to electrical impulses. A direct detector (x-ray to photoconductor to signal) is older and uncommon in CBCT. An indirect detector is the most common with CBCT: x-rays → visible light → photoconductor → signal.

There are three kinds of indirect detectors: flat panel TFT (thin-film transistor) arrays, the most common; CMOS, newer but less common; and CCD, less common.

The flat panel detector

  • Outer layer, the scintillator: a material such as thallium-doped cesium iodide converts each x-ray photon into visible light, in proportion to its intensity.
  • Middle layer, the thin-film transistor layer: an array of photodiodes, receptors of light that each generate an electric signal in proportion to the light reaching them. Each receptor is a pixel (picture element).
  • Inner layer: electronics that amplify and encode the signals.

Because x-rays can't be focused, the detector has to be the same size as the image. Reducing the pixel size increases resolution but leaves fewer photons per pixel, worsening the signal-to-noise ratio; better resolution with low noise takes more dose. The ability of a pixel to distinguish changes from light to dark is its dynamic range, described as gray scale resolution and measured in bit depth (most systems are 14 or 16 bit). Higher bit depth gives finer distinctions as bone changes, at a cost: it's one of the things that drives up the price of a machine.

ROI, FoV and ALARA

  • Region of interest (ROI): the scan volume you want, the area within the field of view that you need to study.
  • Field of view (FoV): the cylindrical volume the machine forms around its axis of rotation, determined mainly by the CBCT's size, movement and the collimation of the beam. It can be set to different sizes, and that changes the patient's dose.
  • ALARA recommends using only the FoV you need. If the FoV is smaller than the ROI, several volumes can be stitched or blended together.

Acquisition

The patient is centered between source and detector, and as the gantry rotates the beam is attenuated through the patient and a single image is collected: a basis image. Several hundred basis images (128-1024, depending on the gantry rate and the detector's frame rate) are captured in one rotation and later reconstructed into the projection volume. Scans typically take 5-40 seconds. More basis images improve the signal-to-noise ratio and reduce scatter, but raise the dose and the reconstruction time.

Processing

Reconstruction turns the basis images into volumetric data through a series of complex mathematical transformations and algorithms: corrections for pixel defects and uneven exposure, a sinogram made by the Radon transformation, and then the Feldkamp-Davis-Kress (FDK) algorithm, a filtered back-projection. It takes 1-20 minutes.

In the image matrix, each cell is a pixel (picture element); when the matrix is reconstructed into a volume, each cell is a voxel (volume element). A CBCT voxel is isotropic, a cube (typically 0.09-0.4 mm), so the volume can be viewed accurately in any direction.

The data are usually proprietary, so they're exported in a standard format, DICOM (Digital Imaging and Communications in Medicine), used for all kinds of medical imaging, including CT and MRI. Viewing software then shows:

  • The three orthoplanar views: axial, sagittal and coronal, plus multiplanar views at any angle.
  • The two common views along the dental arch: panoramic and cross-sectional.
  • 3-D surface reconstructions, to show the surface contours of a structure. Multiplanar views are accurate for linear measurements; 3-D surface reconstructions are not recommended for measuring.

Sharpness and resolution

Geometric unsharpness (the penumbra, "almost shadow") depends on the focal spot size (smaller is sharper), the source-to-object distance and the object-to-detector distance; the gantry has to clear the patient's head and shoulders, which is why C-shaped gantries are common. Spatial resolution depends mainly on voxel size and focal spot, and also on the beam geometry, scatter, patient movement, detector blur, the number of projections and the reconstruction algorithm.

Artifacts

An artifact is any distortion or error in the image unrelated to the subject. Medical CT has fewer than CBCT, because of its higher energies, geometry and lower noise.

  • Scatter: diffracted x-rays cause streaking and grainy noise.
  • Partial volume averaging: a voxel bigger than the object averages bone and soft tissue into a gray that represents neither; choose the smallest voxel.
  • Cone-beam effect: distortion at the edges of the volume from the beam's divergence.
  • Under-sampling: too few basis images: misregistration, fine striations (aliasing, a moiré effect).
  • Beam hardening: as the beam passes through an object, lower-energy photons are absorbed in preference to higher-energy ones. It shows as cupping (distortion of metallic structures) or as white streaks or dark bands between two dense objects (extinction or missing-value artifacts). Manage it by reducing the field size, changing the patient's position and separating the arches; newer machines add artifact-reduction algorithms.
  • Patient motion: misregistration that appears as double contours, easier to cause with small voxels. Minimized by a head restraint and a short scan time.

Contrast also suffers from scattered radiation, the heel effect (more noise on the cathode side) and detector problems such as saturation, dark current and bad pixels.

Gray values and Hounsfield units

Contrast is a range of grays from white to black. In multi-slice (medical) CT, gray values are calibrated to the Hounsfield unit (HU) scale, which describes a voxel's x-ray attenuation relative to air (-1000) and water (0). In CBCT the HU scale is unreliable, because of the scatter of the cone-beam geometry and data truncation; values are uncertain and inconsistent, especially in low-contrast soft tissue, so use them with caution. For example, predicting the stability of an immediately placed and loaded implant from CBCT Hounsfield values is unreliable. (The study guide: "unreliable (but still helpful) for treatment decisions, such as for immediate loading.")
readings.surgery:
What's tested
  • How osseointegration is defined, and what it looks like clinically (about 60% bone contact)
  • Early vs late implant failures, and what causes each
  • Peri-implant health, peri-implant mucositis and peri-implantitis: the case definitions
  • The risk factors for peri-implant disease, and how well it can be treated
  • Pre-surgical assessments and contraindications
  • Prosthetic space for each type of prosthesis
  • Esthetic risk factors
  • The surgical armamentarium: sequential drilling, heat, torque and stability

Dr. Mia Geisinger, Professor and Chair of Periodontology and Director of its advanced program, gave this lecture ("Don't have a screw loose!") on November 2. Her objectives: weigh the risks and benefits of implant-supported restorations, the criteria for implant success in the short and long term, how procedures change for particular patients and sites, and the armamentarium and general steps of placement.

Why implants

About 178 million Americans are missing at least one tooth, about 40 million are missing all their teeth, and 30% of people aged 65-74 are completely edentulous (American College of Prosthodontists, 2015). About 5 million implants are placed in the U.S. each year. Success means health, function and esthetics, and it depends on the bone, the soft tissue, the implant, the surgical technique and the restoration.

An implant is an ankylosed tooth

The tissue around an implant differs from the tissue around a tooth: the collagen fibers run parallel and circular to the abutment instead of obliquely into a root, and the implant is held by ankylosis (osseointegration), with no periodontal ligament. The peri-implant mucosa facing the abutment has two parts: a coronal sulcular epithelium with a thin barrier epithelium (like the junctional epithelium of gingiva), about 1.5-2 mm; and an apical connective tissue adhesion zone, about 1-1.5 mm, where connective tissue lies directly on the abutment. That long junctional epithelium is more susceptible to breakdown over time, so implants are more susceptible to disease.

Because it can't move, an implant appears to move as the jaws keep growing through life: in perimenopause and menopause, for example, hormonal changes reshape the mandible and implants can seem to drift lingually and distally, or end up out of occlusion. That's why implants aren't placed in growing patients, and why pregnancy and menopause deserve thought. For the same reason a probing depth number alone doesn't diagnose an implant: a 5 mm reading may be normal for its placement depth. Increasing depths over time are what matter, so monitor implants with measurements over time.

Osseointegration: two definitions

  • Brånemark et al., 1969: an intimate bone-to-implant contact at a light microscopic level.
  • Albrektsson and Sennerby, 1991: a direct structural and functional connection between living bone and the surface of a load-carrying implant. "Living" matters: a xenograft particle touching an implant isn't alive, so it isn't supporting it.

The clinical realities, from animal and human studies: only about 60% of a roughened implant's surface shows mineralized bone contact, even in a healthy implant; that contact stops about 0.3 mm from the implant-abutment interface (because of micromovement and bacteria there); and integration takes 6 weeks to 3 months of healing. Bone right next to an implant has no nerve endings, so if a patient jumps when you tighten a component, you're on soft tissue.

Early and late failures

Early failures are generally related to:

  • Surgical failures: too much force placing the implant, too much speed and not enough irrigation, overheating the bone (massive necrosis), contaminating the site with a non-aseptic technique.
  • Occlusal overload: heavy forces before osseointegration has reached secondary stability.
  • Impaired wound healing.
  • Poor bone metabolism or turnover.

Late failures are generally related to:

  • Biologic complications: peri-implant mucositis and peri-implantitis. There's good evidence that many are iatrogenic.
  • Occlusal overload.
  • Prosthetic complications.

How well can we treat peri-implant disease?

Not well. Current peri-implantitis therapies show short-term benefits at best; some interventions report recurrence of up to 100% after 12 months; overall, 75% of peri-implantitis cases remain unresolved or recur within 5 years (Heitz-Mayfield and Mombelli 2014; Esposito 2012; Heitz-Mayfield 2018). If root canals failed 75% of the time, we wouldn't do them (they succeed about 86% at 10 years). So "it is imperative that dental healthcare providers seek to center prevention of peri-implant disease as an integral part of implant therapy."

Peri-implant health, mucositis and peri-implantitis

Healthy peri-implant mucosa (histologically) has a core of connective tissue covered by keratinized or non-keratinized epithelium; it is about 3-4 mm tall with an epithelial attachment about 2 mm long, and small clusters of inflammatory (surveillance) cells sit next to the barrier epithelium. The case definitions (Renvert et al., 2018):

ConditionFindings
Peri-implant healthNo inflammation; no profuse bleeding on probing; probing depths may differ with placement depth and soft tissue height but don't increase over time; no further bone loss after initial healing (which should not be 2 mm or more)
Peri-implant mucositisSigns of inflammation (erythema, edema, changes in color, contour and consistency); profuse bleeding and/or suppuration on probing; increased probing depths vs baseline; no bone loss beyond the crestal changes of initial remodeling
Peri-implantitisInflammation plus bleeding and/or suppuration on probing; increasing probing depths vs baseline; progressive bone loss compared with the radiographic bone level 1 year after the prosthesis was delivered
Peri-implantitis, no baseline recordsRadiographic bone level 3 mm or more from the most coronal part of the implant and/or probing depths of 6 mm or more, plus profuse bleeding

Mucositis compared with gingivitis (Heitz-Mayfield and Salvi 2018): both are inflammation without bone (or attachment) loss, but experimental mucositis produces a greater increase in bleeding sites than experimental gingivitis, may take longer than 3 weeks to reverse clinically (although biomarkers resolve after 21 days of restored biofilm control), and after 3 months of plaque in dogs the inflammation is more pronounced around implants than around teeth. People are high or low responders to plaque either way.

Risk factors for peri-implant disease

CategoryFactors
Patient-relatedOral hygiene; professional maintenance; systemic diseases; tobacco use; systemic medications
Implant-relatedImplant design and surface characteristics; titanium dissolution products
Implant site-relatedPrevious unresolved endodontic infection; previous implant failure; periodontal phenotype
Prosthetic-relatedResidual cement; occlusal overload; prosthetic contours
Surgical-relatedImplant malpositioning; non-adherence to surgical protocols; post-operative healing

Implants are harder to keep clean than teeth because of their shape: there's more negative space in the peri-implant pocket. Old hydroxyapatite-coated implants integrated quickly, but once exposed to the mouth the coating dissolved, and bone loss progressed rapidly once peri-implantitis began. Titanium dissolution products can also change how the bacteria around implants behave. Site factors include the soft tissue thickness, the bone volume and the reason the tooth was lost.

Primary prevention of peri-implantitis: risk assessment, treatment planning, implant site development (hard and soft tissue, and restorative space) and regular maintenance. Dr. Geisinger finds "prosthetically driven" incomplete: implants should be prosthetically driven and biologically executed, with a top-down plan that starts from the tooth and builds the structures around it. About 80% of the implants she places today get soft tissue grafting at the same time.

Contraindications

Implants are an elective procedure, so the absolute contraindications are the risks of any elective procedure: a high-risk patient (a recent heart attack or stroke), heavy nicotine use (the equivalent of 10 or more cigarettes a day, "generally a contraindication"), and patients who are still growing. Poor oral hygiene matters too.

Pre-surgical assessments

  • Patient level: medical and dental history; tobacco use; age and growth; hormonal influences; oral hygiene; parafunctional habits and occlusion; smile line; neuromuscular conditions; why the teeth were lost (caries vs perio); esthetic expectations; finances.
  • Site: the size, shape and position of the tooth to be replaced; anatomical landmarks; bone volume and position (resorption in three dimensions); the skeletal relationship; vertical dimension; soft tissue volume, contours and quality; prosthetic space.
  • Implant: position; length and width relative to the tooth being replaced; number of implants; A-P spread; whether they need splinting.
  • Surgical: site assessment and any previous site preparation; anatomical concerns; restoration type; the implant system and its sequential drilling protocol; site-specific bone density; the placement torque; and positioning bucco-lingually, mesio-distally and apico-coronally.

Implant size changed with experience: Dr. Geisinger was once taught to drill a 25 mm implant down to the lower border of the mandible for bicortical stabilization. Today we know that implants over 13.5 mm have a higher failure rate than implants of 8-13 mm: "longer and wider is not always better."

Guides and imaging

A surgical/radiographic guide is stabilized on the remaining dentition, gives accurate information for placing the implant in the required restorative position in three dimensions (bucco-lingual position, vertical position and angulation), and allows verification. Without an idea of the occlusal scheme and the prosthesis design, the radiographic assessment has no target. Imaging runs from 2-D (periapical, panoramic, occlusal, cephalometric) to tomography (CT/CBCT, MRI). The location and quality of the bone affect the implant's angulation, the prosthetic design and long-term success, and a minimum of 1.0 mm of bone is needed buccally and lingually at placement, more in the esthetic zone.

Compared with freehand placement, CBCT-aided placement means less post-operative pain and fewer complications, less need for onlay or simultaneous grafting, and longer implants planned in posterior sites than when planning from a pan (Pozzi, Chan, Guerrero 2014). Know the scan's voxel size and slice spacing (often 0.1 or 0.3 mm): smaller voxels and closer slices mean more radiation. Static and dynamic guides both deviate significantly less from the plan than freehand placement: about 1.0-1.2 mm at the platform, about 1.3 mm at the apex and about 3.5 degrees of angle (static 1.16 mm, 1.3 mm, 3.43 degrees; dynamic 1.02 mm, 1.33 mm, 3.59 degrees).

Space matters in every direction. Implants placed closer than 3 mm lose the peak of bone between them, and the papilla with it: an esthetic issue, not a safety one. An implant set right at the crest of a site with 15 mm of height, under a molar, gives a "candy apple on a stick" emergence; it needs apico-coronal room to flare out.

ProsthesisMinimal vertical space
Non-splinted overdenture10-12 mm

Implant fixed crown and bridge7-8 mm cement-retained; 7.5 mm screw-retained

Turned around, by the space available: under 10 mm, only fixed crown and bridge (no hybrid, no removable); 10-12 mm, crown and bridge or monolithic/layered zirconia, or a non-splinted overdenture (a bar overdenture is contraindicated); 12-15 mm, crown and bridge with pink porcelain, zirconia, or either overdenture; 15 mm or more, a hybrid (metal framework with acrylic) or a combination bridge, or either overdenture, but conventional crown and bridge is contraindicated. Sometimes it's best to start from the space available and design backward.
