Alveolar boneNo deficiencyHorizontal deficiencyVertical deficiency

A very narrow space, or a wide one with several implants side by side, makes full papilla fill unlikely.

What edentulism does to the jaws

  • Decreased height and width of the supporting and basal bone.
  • Increased prominence of the mylohyoid ridge and superior genial tubercles.
  • Increased prominence of the mandibular canal.
  • Relative prominence of the mylohyoid and buccinator muscles.
  • A relative increase in the size of the tongue.
  • Less, and poorer, attached keratinized gingiva.

The armamentarium and drilling

The osteotomy is cut with sequential drills, small to large, at a speed and diameter set by the system and the bone density (soft, normal or hard bone each have their own sequence). Starting with the biggest drill would remove a lot of bone at once, and the friction would overheat what remains: bone heated above 47°C (body temperature is 37°C) suffers thermal necrosis, which can be catastrophic. Copious saline irrigation protects the bone, but in a very deep osteotomy little irrigation reaches the bottom, which may be why long implants fail more. Straumann's protocol starts at about 800 RPM and slows as the drills widen. For a 3.5 mm implant the last drill is 2.8 mm, so the threads engage the bone. The first (pilot) drill is end-cutting with a deep bevel; the rest are side-cutting. Drills carry depth markings, and in the maxilla a wrong depth can reach the nose or brain, so Dr. Geisinger checks her probe against the drill at every change, like a pilot's checklist. The implant itself is threaded in slowly, under a torque (Ncm) setting, not at drilling RPM.

Torque and stability at placement

At placement she generally looks for stability between 15 and 35 Ncm. 35 Ncm is the threshold for putting something transgingival (a healing abutment or provisional through the tissue); an implant with less than 15 Ncm is considered unstable and would spin in the osteotomy. An immediate implant that engages only the palatal bone can still be quite stable. "Finger tight" is about 15 Ncm; most components are torqued to about 35 Ncm, and over-tightening a healing abutment to 50-70 Ncm can risk the integration when it has to be backed out.
readings.guided:
What's tested
  • Surgically driven vs prosthetically driven implant placement
  • Freehand, static guided (semi-guided/pilot and fully guided) and dynamic guided surgery: how each works, pros and cons
  • Tooth-, tissue- and bone-supported guides, and which is most accurate
  • STL vs DICOM files, and the steps of planning a fully guided case
  • The best implant position in the anterior and posterior, and what to do when it isn't surgically possible
  • How the UAB student clinic does it, and the codes

The course's last PCD lecture of the year (Nov 2), built from Dr. Omar's materials and given by the course director, sorts out two separate questions: where the implant should go (surgically driven or prosthetically driven), and how it gets there (freehand, static guided or dynamic guided surgery).

Surgically driven vs prosthetically driven

The surgeon's job is to find the bone (with a CBCT) and, if there's no bone, to create it (grafting). The restorative dentist's job is to make the impression and restore the implant. An implant placed where the bone happens to be can be surgically okay but restoratively not okay; the reverse happens too. A common surgical mistake is placing the implant too buccally: the soft tissue migrates apically (recession), and the restoration looks wrong. An implant "can be placed almost everywhere (except on a root, a nerve or air), but you need to be able to restore it." It needs to be prosthetically driven (and surgically acceptable).

The best position

  • Posterior: right at the middle of the wax-up or tooth contour: mesio-distally in the middle, and bucco-lingually in the middle, along the long axis.
  • Anterior: mesio-distally along the zenith and the long axis; bucco-lingually at the middle of the lingual surface, above the cingulum.

These best positions may not be surgically feasible (a root, a nerve, air in the way), so communication and compromise are important. Options: accept a position slightly off axis from the plan (it can still be restored, with a cement-retained crown on a custom abutment if the screw channel would otherwise exit facially); grafting; or enameloplasty of the proximal or opposing teeth to make room. If enameloplasty will be needed, decide before the implant goes in; taking 2-3 mm off natural teeth is too much (it exposes dentin and causes sensitivity).

Freehand surgery

The traditional method: no guide, relying on the surgeon's experience and common sense. A CBCT is still needed (in the old days it was a PA and pano). Freehand surgery tends to follow where the bone is: it is surgically driven.

  • Advantage: cost-effective (the patient doesn't pay for a guide).
  • Disadvantages: no input from the restorative dentist if the surgeon isn't restoring it; a higher risk of error in depth, angulation and position, with pain, infection and potential implant failure (an implant hitting a neighboring root, or crowding a tooth despite plenty of room); a steeper learning curve for inexperienced clinicians.
  • Freehand can still achieve a good result with frequent verification of the drilling axis, intraorally or by x-ray (a guide pin or the drill left in the channel, then a PA before enlarging it), and with the prosthetic plan in mind.

The surgical guide is how you communicate

Static guided surgery uses a fixed guide, in two kinds:

  • Semi-guided (pilot-guided) surgery uses a surgical template (stent). We don't know what the bone looks like underneath (the guide is a wax-up on the model, a suck-down and a tube, made without considering the bone), but it tells the surgeon where the best position for the implant is. It guides only the pilot drill; after that the surgeon can alter the axis or depth to fit the bone, freehand. This is what the UAB student clinic does most of the time.
  • Fully guided surgery: the axis and depth are designed in software from the CBCT and a digital wax-up, and the guide controls every drill. The surgeon can't alter the implant position unless they remove the guide. Sleeves, a stop key and a drilling protocol control the depth, angulation and location of placement.

How a guide is supported

SupportNote
Tooth-supportedMost accurate
Tissue-supportedTissue is soft, so the guide can move
Bone-supportedBuilt from the CBCT, so it may carry distortion

Planning a fully guided case

It takes two kinds of scan files:

  • STL (Standard Tessellation Language): a surface scan of the teeth and soft tissue, from an intraoral scanner or from scanning gypsum models.
  • DICOM (Digital Imaging and Communications in Medicine): the medical image file, the CBCT (bone, soft tissue, nerve, sinus).

Why both? A CBCT captures little soft tissue, and radiopaque restorations (zirconia, amalgam) scatter and blur the contours of the teeth, so the surface scan supplies an accurate picture of the dentition. The steps:

  1. Intraoral impression (digital or conventional) → the digital file of the dentition (STL).
  2. CBCT → the DICOM file (bone, soft tissue, nerve, sinus).
  3. Mount the models and wax up (digitally).
  4. Align the STL file and the CBCT scan together in the software.
  5. Implant planning.
  6. Design the surgical guide.
  7. Print the guide.

A printed guide has an inspection window to confirm it's fully seated, sleeves that fit the stop key, and a reference such as the midline to confirm it's seated correctly. Guides can be one piece, two pieces (starting tissue-supported) or stackable (starting tooth-supported), and full-arch cases can be pinned in place before the teeth are removed ("Smile in a Box").

  • Advantages: high accuracy if seated correctly; reduced surgery time.
  • Disadvantages: higher cost (software, training, printer, printing resin); a learning curve for the workflow; longer preparation time (planning, printing, post-processing); and "blind surgery": over-trusting the guide can be risky, and the skill of spotting and accommodating a surprise is still needed.

In the UAB student clinic

To encourage guided surgery, the clinic gives extra crown credits (up to two). Codes: D6190 (radiographic/surgical implant index) $50; D6190GS (guided surgery implant index) $225. In the clinic workflow there's no intraoral scan for the impression: you need a high-quality alginate impression and casts mounted on an articulator. A conventional wax-up isn't needed for the guide (the wax-up is digital), but you still wax up before the final crown.

Dynamic guided surgery

Dynamic guided surgery uses no guide: implant placement is controlled in real time by computer navigation. There's no static guide; the clinician watches and adjusts the implant's position on a screen as it's placed. X-Guide tracks the handpiece optically against the plan; Yomi is a robotic system whose arm moves freely until it's within a few millimeters of the site, then physically guides the handpiece and stops you if the angle is off the plan.

MethodGuideWho controls the positionKey points
FreehandNoneThe surgeon, following the boneCheap; surgically driven; higher risk of error; still needs a CBCT
Semi-guided (pilot)Static templateGuide for the pilot drill, then the surgeonBone not known; what UAB students do most
Fully guidedStatic printed guideThe guide, for every drillCBCT + digital wax-up; accurate if seated; costly; "blind surgery" risk
Dynamic guidedNone (navigation)The clinician, watching a screen in real timeX-Guide, Yomi

The summary: CBCT is the current standard of care for most implant cases, because of its superior ability to capture 3-D images of the bone and surrounding structures.

readingsPlain.evolution:
What's tested
  • The seven types of implants, and how to spot each one
  • Why old materials failed and titanium works
  • How osseointegration was found
  • What went wrong with the old designs

The one thing to know

Dr. Mueninghoff, a retired prosthodontist, said the one thing to know from this lecture is the seven types of implants, well enough to recognize them. The stories are background.

Why old materials failed

Gold (1809), lead (1888), platinum and porcelain (1891) were all tried. Gold and platinum have almost no surface oxide, so bone won't grow onto them. Porcelain broke. Titanium works because it is covered in titanium oxide, a ceramic, and bone bonds to that oxide.

Who found osseointegration

Brånemark, a Swedish orthopedic surgeon (a physician), found that titanium pieces he put in animals wouldn't come out: the bone had grown onto them. Carl Misch later made implants popular in the U.S.

The seven types

  • Subperiosteal: a metal frame laid on top of the bone, under the periosteum. Took two surgeries and destroyed bone when it failed.
  • Endodontic stabilizer: a rod through a root canal, out the tip into bone. Made of steel, leaked, failed.
  • Transosseous: goes all the way through the front of the lower jaw, from a plate under the chin. Done in the operating room.
  • Intramucosal insert: buttons on a denture that fit holes made in the gums. The denture couldn't stay out more than a few hours.
  • Blade: a flat blade in a slot in the bone, usually tied to a natural tooth, with soft tissue around it instead of bone.
  • Ramus frame: one big frame from the chin back into both sides of the lower jaw, holding a lower denture.
  • Root form: the screw-shaped titanium implant used today.

Names to know

The Roberts brothers (California) invented the ramus frame and the blade. Linkow put holes in the blade, and Cranin made an anchor-shaped one. Bosker made the transmandibular implant (TMI). In Birmingham, Dr. Ford Turner made ramus frames last 10 to 25 years because he was so careful with the bone.

The old idea of success

Before Brånemark, an implant "worked" if it lasted five years in 75% of patients.

Other lessons

  • Bone only grows about half a millimeter into holes, so hollow baskets didn't lock in.
  • Cementing the abutment into the implant (Core-Vent) made it impossible to remove.
  • A soft insert meant to copy the ligament (IMZ) moved too much and hurt the tooth.
  • Bone near the top needs some load, or it shrinks (stress shielding); Frialit made the top wider for that.
  • Force keeps bone healthy: bone grew thicker behind the TMI plate.
  • Osseointegration is much stronger than people thought, so short implants (8 or even 6 mm) work now.
  • There are about 173 implant companies. Stick with two or three. To identify an unknown one from an x-ray, try whatimplantisthat.com.
readingsPlain.intro:
What's tested
  • What an implant is and what osseointegration means
  • Primary and secondary stability; healing times
  • One-stage vs two-stage surgery
  • Endosteal, subperiosteal and transosteal implants
  • Healthy vs failing implants
  • Titanium grades, the alloy, and each system's surface
  • How the gum attaches to a tooth vs an implant

The course

Dr. Chavali runs this introduction. The school uses three implant systems: Nobel Biocare (Conical Connection), Straumann (Bone Level) and BioHorizons (Tapered Internal). In the lab you restore an implant at tooth #9.

What an implant is

A man-made (alloplastic) device put into the bone, under the gum, to hold and support a crown, bridge or denture. An abutment goes on the implant, and the crown goes on the abutment.

What implants are used for

Single crowns, bridges, partial dentures that clip onto implants, and lower dentures. Two implants under a lower denture are the standard of care for a toothless lower jaw. At UAB this is "2-2-2": two dentures, two implants, two attachments (Locators). The lower jaw gets them because a lower denture floats around; an upper one holds by suction.

Osseointegration

Brånemark (an orthopedic surgeon, 1952) found titanium pieces in rabbit bone wouldn't come out. He named the bond osseointegration: bone attached directly to the implant, with no soft tissue in between.

When the implant is screwed in, it is held by friction: primary stability. Then the bone remodels around it and grows onto it: secondary stability, the real integration. Around the end of the first week, the old bone edges are eaten away, so primary stability drops while new bone builds up.

Usual wait before restoring: about 4 months in the lower jaw, 6 months in the upper jaw, because the lower jaw's bone is denser.

Wolff's law

Bone shapes itself to the forces on it. The right amount of load keeps it strong; too little and it shrinks (as after a tooth is pulled); too much and it breaks down. So implant crowns are adjusted carefully.

One-stage vs two-stage

  • Two-stage (Brånemark): implant placed, cover screw on, gum closed over it for 3-6 months. A second surgery uncovers it and puts on a healing abutment.
  • One-stage (Schroeder): the healing abutment goes on at the start and sticks through the gum. No second surgery; about 3-4 months.
  • Wait at least 3 weeks for the gum to heal around the healing abutment before the final impression.
  • Two-stage is safer when healing is a worry (for example, diabetes).

Three kinds of implants

  • Endosteal: in the bone, through only one layer of cortical bone. Today's screw-shaped root forms, and also the old blades and ramus frames.
  • Eposteal (subperiosteal): on top of the bone, under the periosteum. Hard to remove, big surgery, bone loss.
  • Transosteal: all the way through the front of the lower jaw (the TMI). Lower jaw and front only, a cut under the chin, general anesthesia.

Healthy or failing

Signs of a failing implant: it moves, it hurts when tapped or used, it's infected, there's a dark area around it on the x-ray, or bone is lost. A healthy one has no pain, no movement, less than 2 mm of bone loss and no pus. Losing more than half the implant's length of bone, or any mobility, means failure. Always take an x-ray before you make the crown.

Causes: overheating the bone during surgery, the implant moving while it heals, overloading, infection (peri-implantitis), smoking, uncontrolled diabetes, and poor upkeep.

Titanium

Titanium covers itself with a tough oxide layer, and bone cells build onto it. That's why it doesn't corrode and the body accepts it. There are four grades of commercially pure titanium (stronger as the grade goes up; implants use Grade 4) and a stronger alloy, Ti-6Al-4V. BioHorizons uses the alloy; Straumann and Nobel use Grade 4.

Shape and surface

Old implants were smooth cylinders; screw-shaped (machined) implants hold better. Modern ones are also roughened. Rough surfaces are made by adding (plasma spray, hydroxyapatite, beads) or by taking away (acid etching, blasting). Nobel's surface is TiUnite, Straumann's is SLA (sandblasted, large-grit, acid-etched), and BioHorizons' is RBT (resorbable blast texturing).

Why implants

They keep the bone from shrinking, spare the neighboring teeth, and let a denture bite harder than a regular denture.

An implant is not a tooth

  • A tooth can move a little; an implant can't. It's like a tooth fused to bone.
  • Don't join an implant to a tooth, don't place one in a growing child, and don't hang a cantilever off one implant.
  • The gum fibers around an implant run around it and along it, but none attach into it. Around a tooth, fibers run into the root.
  • The gum seal on an implant is about 3 mm tall, about 1 mm taller than on a tooth.
  • The gum attaches to a tooth along the whole junctional epithelium, but on an implant only at the bottom third.
  • No ligament means no feeling of biting pressure, so implant crowns are kept in light contact.
readingsPlain.biomech:
What's tested
  • Wolff's law and stress = force/area
  • Upper vs lower jaw bone, and D1-D4
  • Which forces bone handles best
  • Cantilevers and long bridges
  • Bite force with different dentitions
  • Why an implant is never joined to a tooth
  • How implant crowns should bite

Bone follows force

Wolff's law: bone rebuilds its inside to match the forces on it. The right amount of load keeps bone healthy. Too little (a missing tooth) and it shrinks; too much (grinding, a bad design) and it breaks down or fractures. Stress = force divided by area; strain is how much the bone bends.

Upper vs lower jaw

The upper jaw has thin outer bone and fine spongy bone; it spreads force out (so a blow to the face doesn't reach the brain). The lower jaw has thick outer bone; it absorbs force. Implants fail more in the upper jaw.

Misch's bone types: D1 (dense, front of lower jaw), D2 (back of lower jaw), D3 (front of upper jaw), D4 (soft, back of upper jaw). D1 is the strongest, D4 the weakest.

Which forces bone likes

Bone is strongest under compression (pushing), then tension (pulling), and weakest under shear (sliding). So aim forces straight down the implant.

What goes wrong

Anything can fail: the bone, the implant, the screw, the crown. Overdenture attachments have the most problems (30%), then resin veneers (22%), short implants (17%) and soft bone (16%). Implants themselves fracture rarely (1-2%). Implants shorter than 10 mm fail a little more often but are still used.

Match the implant to the tooth: about 3 mm for lateral and lower incisors, 3.5 mm for upper centrals, 3.5-4 mm for premolars, 4.5-6 mm for molars. Leave at least 1 mm of bone around it; if the bone is too thin, graft it.

Who bites hardest

Generally younger, bigger patients and men, and anyone who grinds or clenches (look for worn or broken teeth, abfractions, bony growths). For them: more implants, smaller chewing surfaces, splint the implants together, and a night guard.

Don't splint implants on both sides of the lower jaw behind the mental foramina: the lower jaw flexes when it opens.

Cantilevers

A cantilever is a tooth hanging off the end with nothing under it. It acts like a lever: force x distance. In his example a 25 lb bite became 75 lb on one implant and 50 lb on the other. Avoid them (unless the other jaw is a denture). A vertical cantilever is a very tall crown on lost bone; fix it by growing bone back or adding implants.

Long bridges bend a lot: each extra unit of length makes it cube times as flexible (1, 8, 27). Two implants can carry a three-unit bridge, not usually four.

Bite force

Implant bridge > natural teeth > implant-held denture > regular denture. Without the ligament's sensors, patients can bite harder on implants without feeling it.

Never join an implant to a tooth

A tooth can sink 25-100 microns into its ligament; an implant only 3-5 microns. Join them and the implant takes all the force. This will be on the exam.

How implant crowns should bite

  • Lighter than the natural teeth.
  • Implant against a natural tooth: shimstock pulls through on the implant when the patient closes normally; it may hold when they bite hard.
  • Implant against implant: when biting hard, shimstock drags but doesn't tear.
  • Forces straight down the implant, low cusps, a narrow chewing surface, and no contact when sliding side to side.
readingsPlain.terms:
What's tested
  • Brands, product lines, platforms and colors
  • Platform switching, internal vs external, bone vs tissue level, tapered vs parallel
  • Stability and the stability dip; torque numbers
  • Conical connection and Morse taper; cover screw vs healing abutment
  • Where to place an implant (the millimeter rules)
  • Engaging vs non-engaging; screw vs cement; prefab vs custom
  • Space needed; crown-to-implant ratio; E, B and C zones
  • Timeline terms, immediate loading rules, codes

Brands and platforms

Nobel Biocare, Straumann and BioHorizons are brands, and each has several product lines. The platform is where the implant meets the abutment. Within a brand, matching colors mean matching parts. BioHorizons trap: a "4.6 mm Tapered Internal Plus" implant has a 3.5 mm (yellow) platform, not 4.5. The surgeon writes the body size; you need the platform size. Check the implant's sticker in the chart.

Design terms

  • Platform switching: the abutment is narrower than the implant, so the joint (microgap) sits away from the bone. Saves bone and adds gum thickness.
  • External connection: the implant has a hex sticking up (more screw loosening). Internal: the connection is inside the implant (less gap). The school uses internal.
  • Tissue level: a smooth collar sits in the gum; less bone loss. Bone level: more room to shape a nice crown.
  • Tapered: more primary stability, less chance of hitting a root or nerve. Parallel-walled: more surface touching bone.
  • Conical connection: the abutment's tapered surface wedges into the implant; less gap, less bone loss. A Morse taper is a conical connection tight enough to "cold weld."

Stability

Primary stability (the screw's grip) drops as bone remodels; secondary stability (new bone) rises. The low point in between is the stability dip, a few weeks after placement. Be careful touching the implant then.

Torque

Fingers give only about 5 Ncm; use a torque wrench. Nobel 35 Ncm (its 3.0 mm implant 15), Straumann 35 Ncm, BioHorizons 30 Ncm.

Cover screw vs healing abutment

A cover screw is short and hidden under the gum (first stage of two-stage). A healing abutment is taller and sticks through the gum (one-stage, or the second stage).

Where the implant goes

  • Top of the implant 3-4 mm below where the gum line should be.
  • 1.5 mm from a tooth, 3 mm from another implant (or the papilla is lost).
  • 2 mm of bone on the facial (the thin facial bone shrinks after extraction), 1 mm on the lingual.
  • Front teeth: placed a little toward the tongue, so the screw hole can come out the back of the crown. Back teeth: in the middle of the ridge.

Abutments

  • Engaging abutments lock into the implant's hex or grooves and can't spin; non-engaging can spin.
  • Screw-retained: crown and abutment are one piece, screwed in, easy to remove, no cement. Cement-retained: the crown is cemented onto the abutment; no hole showing. If the implant is too far facial, cement it (or use an angled screw channel).
  • Screwmentable: a zirconia crown glued to a TiBase outside the mouth, then screwed in.
  • Prefabricated abutments are stock sizes; custom ones are shaped for the patient and are always engaging.
  • Rules for the clinic: single crown always engaging; cemented bridge: custom, engaging; screwed bridge: TiBase, non-engaging.

Space

A cemented molar crown needs about 7 mm from bone to the opposing tooth (3 for the gum seal, minus 1 below the gum, plus 4 of abutment, plus 1 of zirconia). A screwmentable crown needs about 6-7 mm from the platform.

Implant crowns can be taller than a tooth's crown-to-root rule allows, but very tall ones (about 2:1) loosen and break more: consider splinting.

Emergence profile

The shape of the crown and abutment from the implant up to the gum line. C zone (first 1-1.5 mm, straight, set by the abutment), B zone (middle, concave preferred), E zone (last 1 mm under the gum, set by esthetics). Make it more concave to let the gum creep down; more convex to push it up.

Odds and ends

  • Seal the screw hole with Teflon tape, leave 2 mm, and fill with composite.
  • A verification jig checks that implants for a bridge are where the cast says, using non-engaging parts. The one-screw (Sheffield) test checks passive fit.
  • Open-tray impressions are more accurate for several implants; the clinic mostly uses closed tray.
  • Anodizing colors titanium by thickening its oxide layer.

Timeline terms (ITI 2018)

  • Placement: immediate (same day as extraction), early (4-8 or 12-16 weeks), late (after 6 months).
  • Loading: immediate (within 1 week), early (1 week to 2 months), conventional (after 2 months).
  • A temporary crown on the day of surgery doesn't have to be in function. If you don't need to load it, don't.
  • Immediate loading needs intact socket walls, at least 1 mm of facial bone, thick tissue, no acute infection, bone beyond the socket, 25-40 Ncm torque or ISQ over 70, a protective bite and a compliant patient.

Codes

D0367 CBCT; D6190 implant index; D6010 implant placement; D6057 custom abutment; D6058 cemented implant crown; D6065 screw-retained implant crown; D6245 pontic.
readingsPlain.prefab:
What's tested
  • Stock (prefabricated) vs custom abutments
  • Cover screw, healing abutment, temporary and final abutments
  • One-stage vs two-stage, and who gets which
  • UCLA vs CAD/CAM abutments
  • Cemented vs screwed crowns and the 5 mm rule
  • What to send the lab

Two kinds of abutments

Prefabricated (stock) abutments come ready-made and fit anyone. Custom abutments are made for one patient. The clinic uses custom almost every time.

The parts in order

  • At surgery: a cover screw (under the gum) or a healing abutment (through the gum).
  • Then a temporary abutment for a provisional crown, screwed or cemented.
  • Finally a final abutment: stock, or custom (UCLA cast or CAD/CAM milled).

One-stage vs two-stage

Two-stage: cover screw, gum closed; months later a second surgery puts on the healing abutment. One-stage: the healing abutment goes on right away. Smokers and diabetics get two-stage; young, healthy patients can get one-stage. Wait about three weeks after the healing abutment goes on for the gum to heal.

Healing abutments

They come in heights (short for a shallow implant, tall for a deep one) and shapes: straight for incisors, wide for molars.

Temporary abutments

Screw-retained temporaries are titanium cylinders; cement-retained ones have a plastic cap. Engaging ones have a hex that locks in; non-engaging ones are smooth and are used for bridges. Screwed temporaries avoid extra cement, which acts like tartar and causes peri-implantitis.

Stock vs custom

  • Stock: fits very precisely, cheap (about $50, sometimes free), strong. But it must be trimmed, its margin can end up deep under the gum and trap cement, and its thin shape doesn't support a wide molar crown.
  • Custom: margin wherever you want it, a good shape out of the gum, and easy cement cleanup. About $150-200.

Stock abutments come in cuff heights (1, 2, 3, 5 mm) and straight or angled. Measure the gum height from the implant collar. A tilted implant needs an angled stock abutment or a custom one.

UCLA vs CAD/CAM

A UCLA abutment is a plastic sleeve on a titanium base that the lab waxes up and casts in metal. A CAD/CAM abutment is designed on a computer and milled.

Cemented vs screwed crowns

  • Cemented: often better looking, but much higher risk of peri-implantitis.
  • Screwed: no cement, so no cement problems.
  • Exam rule: if there's 5 mm of space or less between the arches, you must use a screw-retained crown. A cemented crown needs at least 5 mm.
  • If the implant is so far facial that the screw hole would show, you must cement.

What to send the lab

Mounted casts with a soft tissue model, the implant system, the diameter, the soft tissue height, and the implant order form.

The school's systems

BioHorizons (internal connection), Nobel Biocare (conical connection) and Straumann (bone level).
readingsPlain.imaging:
What's tested
  • Dr. Givan's study guide: imaging in the three phases
  • The three common x-ray types and ALARA
  • Pros and cons of PAs and pans
  • Medical CT vs cone beam CT; Hounsfield units
  • CT advantages, problems and artifacts
  • Scan templates and planning software

Plan from the teeth

Dr. Givan's theme: implants are there to hold teeth, so plan from the final teeth (prosthetically driven) while respecting the bone and nerves (biologically balanced). Study his study guide: the exam asks about its details.

Three phases

  • Before surgery: how much bone, how good, at what angle; where the nerves and other structures are; any disease.
  • During surgery: check position and angle, healing, and that the abutment and crown are right.
  • After the crown: for as long as the implant is there, check the bone level at the top of the implant.

The three common images

Periapical (PA), panoramic, and cone beam CT. Always use the lowest reasonable dose (ALARA). A CBCT is about three pans, or a tenth of a medical CT.

PA vs pan

  • PA: very sharp, but shows no bone width, can't measure bone quality, and can be stretched or distorted. Best for following bone levels over time.
  • Pan: a great overview for screening, but lots of overlap, distortion and changing magnification. Bone height can be off by 30%, and bone width can't be seen at all. Metal balls of known size (4-5 mm) in a template let you correct the height, but only up and down and only where it's in focus.

Medical CT vs cone beam CT

Medical CT: a fan beam, fast spin, you lie down (claustrophobic, soft tissue sags, jaw not in its natural spot), higher dose. Cone beam CT: a cone beam, slow spin, you sit or stand, 5-10 times less dose, but more scatter and poorer soft tissue detail.

Hounsfield units

The Hounsfield scale measures radiodensity. People hoped it would predict how stable an implant will be, but the evidence doesn't support that.

CT: good and bad

Good: accurate measurements in every direction, no distortion, some idea of bone quality, models and drill guides, and even surgery without a flap. Bad: take out metal dentures first; metal fillings scatter; movement blurs.

Artifacts

  • Motion: the patient or template moved.
  • Starburst: streaks where density changes sharply (air to bone, bone to metal). Not caused by scatter.
  • Beam hardening: metal filters out the weak x-rays, leaving black areas.
  • Titanium causes little artifact; gold causes a lot.

Scan templates

A scan template is a temporary set of teeth worn during the scan, so you can see where the new teeth will be compared with the bone. It steadies the bite and opens it slightly. Steps: make the guide, scan, plan in software; optionally print a surgical guide (resting on bone, gum or teeth, with sleeves to steer the drill).

Planning software: Simplant, Implant Design Studio, Nobel Clinician, coDiagnostiX, Invivo, Blue Sky Bio.
readingsPlain.cbct:
What's tested
  • What CBCT stands for and how it works
  • How x-rays are made, filtered and absorbed
  • The four interactions and the two that matter
  • Detectors, pixels, resolution and noise
  • ROI, FoV, ALARA
  • Basis images, voxels, DICOM and the views
  • Artifacts and why CBCT Hounsfield numbers aren't reliable

How a CBCT works

CBCT = cone beam computed tomography. An x-ray source and a detector sit on a rotating arm (the gantry) and turn around the patient's head. A cone-shaped beam passes through the area you want to see. In one turn (180 or 360 degrees) it takes several hundred flat pictures, and a computer combines them into a 3-D volume.

Making x-rays

A heated filament (the cathode) gives off electrons: thermionic emission. The voltage (kVp) speeds them toward a tungsten target (the anode). Higher kVp makes higher-energy x-rays that penetrate more. Almost all the energy becomes heat; about 1% becomes x-rays.

  • Characteristic x-rays: an electron knocks out an inner electron of a tungsten atom; an outer electron drops in and gives off an x-ray of a set energy.
  • Bremsstrahlung ("braking") x-rays: an electron swerves near the nucleus and loses energy as an x-ray of any energy.

So the beam has many energies: it's polyenergetic. A filter (aluminum or copper) removes the weak x-rays that would only add dose, and lead collimator plates shape the beam.

Attenuation

Attenuation is how much the beam weakens as it passes through something. Thicker, denser material with a higher atomic number blocks more. Gold blocks and scatters a lot; titanium much less.

Four things can happen to an x-ray in tissue: it passes straight through; it's absorbed (the photoelectric effect, which ionizes the atom); it bounces off without losing energy (Rayleigh, minor); or it bounces off an electron and loses energy (Compton, which causes artifacts). The two that matter most: absorption and Compton.

Detectors

  • Computed radiography: phosphor plates read by a laser (UAB's PAs and bitewings). Not used for CBCT.
  • Indirect flat panel (the usual CBCT detector): x-rays → light → photodiode → signal. Each light receptor is a pixel.
  • Smaller pixels: sharper image but more noise (worse signal-to-noise ratio).
  • Dynamic range (bit depth) is how finely a pixel tells light from dark: gray-scale resolution.

ROI, FoV, ALARA

The region of interest is what you need to see; the field of view is the cylinder the machine actually scans. A bigger FoV means more dose, so by ALARA scan only what you need.

Processing

Each single picture is a basis image. Hundreds are reconstructed with math into a volume made of voxels (3-D pixels). The file format is DICOM. You can view it axial, sagittal and coronal, as a panoramic slice with cross-sections, or as a 3-D surface (not for measuring).

Artifacts

  • Scatter: streaks.
  • Beam hardening: the weak x-rays get soaked up first, causing dark cups and streaks around metal.
  • Motion: double outlines; prevent with a head rest and a short scan.

Hounsfield units

Medical CT grays are set on the Hounsfield scale (air -1000, water 0). On a CBCT these numbers are unreliable because of scatter, so don't trust them to decide, for example, whether an implant can be loaded right away.
readingsPlain.surgery:
What's tested
  • The two definitions of osseointegration
  • Early vs late failures
  • Health, mucositis and peri-implantitis
  • Risk factors and prevention
  • Contraindications and assessments
  • Space needed for each prosthesis
  • Esthetic risk factors
  • Drilling, heat and torque

The big picture

Dr. Geisinger (periodontology) gave this lecture. About 178 million Americans are missing a tooth and about 5 million implants are placed each year. A good implant is healthy, works and looks good.

Implants are like fused teeth

Gum fibers run around and along an implant, not into it, and there's no ligament. The seal is a long attachment that breaks down more easily than a tooth's. Because an implant can't move, it can look like it moves as the jaws change with age. A single pocket reading doesn't mean much on an implant; watch for depths that increase over time.

Osseointegration

Brånemark (1969): bone touching the implant under a light microscope. Albrektsson (1991): a direct structural and functional connection between living bone and an implant carrying load. In real life only about 60% of the surface touches bone, the bone stops about 0.3 mm below the implant-abutment joint, and healing takes 6 weeks to 3 months.

Early vs late failure

  • Early: surgical mistakes (overheating the bone, too much force, poor sterile technique), loading too soon, poor healing, poor bone turnover.
  • Late: gum and bone disease around the implant, overload, and problems with the crown or bridge.

Peri-implant disease

  • Health: no inflammation, no heavy bleeding, pockets not deepening, no bone loss after the first healing.
  • Mucositis: red, swollen, bleeding or pus, deeper pockets, but no bone loss.
  • Peri-implantitis: inflammation and bleeding plus bone loss compared with the x-ray taken a year after the crown. Without old records: bone 3 mm or more below the top of the implant and/or pockets of 6 mm or more with heavy bleeding.

Treatment works poorly: about 75% of cases don't resolve or come back within 5 years. So prevention is the job: assess risk, plan well, build the site, and keep up maintenance.

Risk factors

Patient: poor hygiene, missed maintenance, systemic disease, smoking, medications. Implant: its design and surface. Site: an old root canal infection, a previous failed implant, thin tissue. Prosthesis: leftover cement, overload, bad contours. Surgery: a badly placed implant, not following the protocol, poor healing.

Contraindications

Implants are elective. Don't place them in someone with a recent heart attack or stroke, a heavy smoker (10 or more cigarettes a day), or a patient still growing.

Planning

Check the patient (health, habits, smile line, expectations, money), the site (bone in three directions, gum, space), and the implant (where, how big, how many). Keep at least 1 mm of bone on the cheek and tongue sides. Implants longer than about 13.5 mm actually fail more than 8-13 mm ones. A CBCT helps avoid complications and grafting.

Space needed

Implant crown or bridge: about 7-8 mm (cemented) or 7.5 mm (screwed). Overdenture: 10-12 mm; bar overdenture 11-14 mm. Zirconia full-arch: 10-12 mm. Hybrid: 15 mm or more.

Esthetic risk

High risk: heavy smoker, weak immune system, high expectations, high lip line, thin scalloped gums, triangular teeth, an acute infection, bone 7 mm or more from the contact point, restored neighbors, a gap of two or more teeth, a gum defect, or vertical bone loss.

Drilling

Drills go from small to large so the bone doesn't overheat: above 47°C the bone dies. Use lots of saline. The last drill is narrower than the implant so the threads bite. Implants are placed slowly with a torque setting, not at high speed.

Stability at placement: 15-35 Ncm. At 35 Ncm you can put something through the gum; under 15 Ncm the implant is unstable.
readingsPlain.guided:
What's tested
  • Surgically vs prosthetically driven
  • Freehand, semi-guided, fully guided and dynamic surgery
  • Which guide support is most accurate
  • STL vs DICOM and the planning steps
  • Best implant positions
  • How the student clinic does it

Where vs how

Two questions: where should the implant go, and how will the surgeon get it there?

Where: let the tooth decide

Surgically driven: put the implant where the bone is. Prosthetically driven: put it where the future tooth needs it, then make sure the bone allows it (graft if not). An implant can go almost anywhere except into a root, a nerve or air, but it has to be restorable. A common mistake is placing it too far toward the cheek, so the gum recedes.

Best positions: back teeth, the middle of the tooth in both directions, along its long axis. Front teeth, in line with the gum's high point (zenith), and toward the tongue side, above the cingulum. If that isn't possible, talk it through: a slightly tilted implant can still get a cemented crown, the bone can be grafted, or neighboring teeth can be reshaped a little (decide before surgery).

How: four ways

  • Freehand: no guide; the surgeon follows the bone. Cheap, but more risk of a wrong depth, angle or position, and no input from the restoring dentist. Still needs a CBCT. Checking with an x-ray during drilling helps.
  • Semi-guided (pilot): a simple guide made on the model shows where the first (pilot) drill goes; then the surgeon adjusts to the bone. This is what UAB students usually do.
  • Fully guided: the whole plan is made in software from the CBCT and a digital wax-up, and a printed guide controls every drill (sleeves and stops set depth and angle). Accurate and quick if the guide seats right, but costly, slower to prepare, and you can't change course without removing the guide.
  • Dynamic: no guide at all; the surgeon watches a screen that tracks the drill live (X-Guide), or a robot arm guides the hand (Yomi).

Guide support

Tooth-supported guides are the most accurate. Tissue-supported ones can move on the soft gum. Bone-supported ones may carry CBCT distortion.

Planning a fully guided case

You need two files: an STL (a surface scan of teeth and gums) and a DICOM (the CBCT). Steps: scan or impress the teeth (STL), take the CBCT (DICOM), mount and wax up, line up the two files in the software, plan the implant, design the guide, print it. The guide has a window to check it's fully seated and a midline to check it's in the right spot.

At UAB

You get extra crown credits for using guided surgery. D6190 (implant index) is $50; D6190GS (guided surgery index) is $225. The clinic uses a good alginate impression and mounted casts, not an intraoral scan.

Bottom line

A CBCT is now the standard of care for most implant cases.
